days.title: Microsoft Entra Users and Groups: Members, Guests, Group Types, and Dynamic Membership

concepts.heading: Members and Guests
concepts.body: Every account in a Microsoft Entra ID tenant has a User type of Member or Guest, and that property is separate from where the person signs in. An internal member is created in your tenant, has a user principal name in one of your domains and a password your tenant manages. A B2B guest is invited by email and signs in with the credentials of their own organization; the account in your tenant gets a name such as ana_fabrikam.com#EXT#@contoso.onmicrosoft.com. Guests have restricted directory permissions by default, so they can manage their own profile but cannot browse the directory like employees. You can change a user from Guest to Member, for example for staff of an acquired subsidiary who keep signing in with their own tenant. On the exam, Member versus Guest decides directory permissions, not how the user authenticates.

concepts.heading: Security Groups and Microsoft 365 Groups
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra ID has two group types. Security groups grant access to resources such as apps, Azure role assignments and SharePoint permissions, and their members can be users, devices or service principals. Microsoft 365 groups are for collaboration: they come with a group email address, a shared mailbox, a calendar and a SharePoint site, and their members can only be users. The group type is fixed when the group is created, so a security group that now needs a shared mailbox is replaced by a new Microsoft 365 group. The option that lets Microsoft Entra roles be assigned to a group can also only be set at creation. A mail-enabled security group, managed in Exchange, distributes email but has no shared mailbox or calendar. If a question asks which group can hold devices, the answer is a security group.

concepts.heading: Assigned and Dynamic Membership
concepts.body: Membership type is the second choice for a group, and unlike group type it can be changed later. With Assigned membership, owners or administrators add members by hand. With Dynamic User or Dynamic Device membership, a rule decides, for example user.department -eq "Sales", and Microsoft Entra ID adds and removes members as attributes change. Nobody can add members to a dynamic group by hand, not even its owner. Rules evaluate -and before -or, so use parentheses or the -in operator with a list of values, and add user.userType -eq "Member" to keep guests out. A device rule can use only device attributes such as deviceOSType and is typed in the rule text box. Dynamic user groups need Microsoft Entra ID P1 for their members. Converting an assigned group to dynamic keeps its object ID, removes members who do not match and adds those who do.

concepts.heading: Bulk Operations
concepts.body: The Microsoft Entra admin center offers bulk operations that take a CSV template downloaded from the same page. Bulk create makes internal member accounts; its required columns are the name, the user name in one of your domains and an initial password, and it sends no email to anyone. Bulk invite creates B2B guests: each row needs the email address to invite and a redirection URL, such as https://myapps.microsoft.com, and the guests receive invitation emails. Bulk delete removes the listed accounts, and Bulk restore on the Deleted users page brings back soft-deleted users listed by object ID. Groups also have a bulk import of members. Each job runs in the background, and failures for single rows appear on the Bulk operation results page. When a scenario needs outside partners to use their own credentials and get an invitation, the answer is Bulk invite, not Bulk create.

concepts.heading: Deleting and Restoring Users and Groups
concepts.body: Deleting a user in Microsoft Entra ID does not remove the account at once. It stays soft-deleted for 30 days on the Deleted users page, and a restore brings it back with its original object ID and properties, so app assignments and references keep working. Licenses that the user had when deleted are restored even if the tenant has no free licenses left, which can leave the tenant above its purchased count until you clean up. After 30 days the account is deleted permanently and nobody, including Microsoft Support, can restore it; you would have to create a new account with a new object ID. Deleted Microsoft 365 groups are also kept for 30 days and can be restored by administrators such as a Groups Administrator, or by the group's own owner. For the exam, remember the 30-day window, that restore beats re-creation, and that Bulk restore takes object IDs.

examPoints: A question that asks why a guest cannot browse the directory, or how to give an external user member-level access, is testing the User type property, which is separate from where the user signs in.

A question that needs a shared mailbox, or that puts devices into a group, is testing group types: collaboration features come only with Microsoft 365 groups, and devices fit only in security groups, and the type cannot change after creation.
A question about a dynamic group that will not accept a manual member, or that includes the wrong users, is testing rule-based membership and the rule that -and is evaluated before -or.

quiz.q: An administrator deleted the account of a sales manager by mistake 12 days ago. She restores it from the Deleted users page. What is the result?
choices: The account comes back with a new object ID, so every app assignment and group reference has to be added again by hand
The account comes back with its original object ID and properties, because deleted users stay restorable for 30 days
The account cannot be restored, because deleted users are kept for only seven days before Microsoft Entra ID removes them
The account comes back as a guest user, because restored accounts lose their member type and must be converted again
quiz.explain: A deleted user stays soft-deleted for 30 days and a restore returns the same object with its properties, which is why restoring beats re-creating. Choice A describes what happens when you create a new account instead, which is exactly the work a restore avoids.

quiz.q: A dynamic group uses the rule user.department -eq "Sales" -or user.department -eq "Support" -and user.country -eq "KR". Sales employees based in Japan appear in the group, although only Korean staff should. Why?
choices: Dynamic rules ignore the country attribute unless the users have a usage location set, so the country check is skipped
The rule processing for the group is paused, so the group still holds members that were added by an earlier version of the rule
Guests from Japan match every dynamic rule until the userType check is added, so they are added by default to the group
The -and operator is evaluated before -or, so the country check applies only to Support; group the departments with parentheses
quiz.explain: Microsoft Entra ID evaluates -and before -or, so the rule reads as Sales, or Support in Korea, and every Sales employee matches. Choice C is tempting because guests are a common rule problem, but these users are employees and the real fault is operator precedence.

days.recap: Users are members or guests regardless of where they sign in, groups are security or Microsoft 365 types fixed at creation with assigned or dynamic membership, and deleted users and Microsoft 365 groups can be restored for 30 days.

days.title: Licenses, External Users, and Self-Service Password Reset

concepts.heading: Group-Based Licensing
concepts.body: Instead of assigning licenses user by user, you can assign a product such as Microsoft 365 E3 to a group, and Microsoft Entra ID applies it to every member in the background. You can also turn off individual service plans in the group's assignment. Two rules matter for the exam. First, licenses are applied only to direct members: if the licensed group contains other groups, the users in those nested groups get nothing, and no error is shown. Second, processing is not instant, so when a user moves from one licensed group to another, add the user to the new group first, confirm the license on the user's Licenses page, and only then remove the old group. Removing first leaves a gap with no mailbox or Teams access. A license comes and goes with group membership, so leaving the group removes the license.

concepts.heading: Usage Location and Licensing Errors
concepts.body: Some services are not available in every country, so a license needs a usage location, a two-letter code such as KR or DE. A direct assignment fails until you set the user's usage location, while group-based licensing falls back to the tenant's location for users who have none. Group licensing reports problems on the group and on the user instead of failing at once. Not enough licenses means the product is used up: buy more or free some, for example unused direct assignments, then select Reprocess. Conflicting service plans means the user already holds a plan that clashes, such as Exchange Online Plan 1 from a direct E1 license next to Plan 2 from E3; remove the redundant direct license or disable one plan, then reprocess. Usage location isn't allowed means a service in the license is not offered in the user's country.

concepts.heading: B2B Collaboration Settings
concepts.body: External collaboration settings in the Microsoft Entra admin center hold three separate controls. Guest user access sets what guests can see in the directory. Guest invite settings decide who may invite, from anyone including guests down to no one at all; the level Only users assigned to specific admin roles lets just User Administrators and holders of the Guest Inviter role invite, and Guest Inviter grants nothing else. Collaboration restrictions decide which domains may be invited, either with a deny list that blocks named domains such as gmail.com or with an allow list that permits only named partner domains. The lists are checked when an invitation is sent and when it is redeemed: a pending invitation to a newly blocked domain fails, but guests who already redeemed keep their accounts until you remove them. If a question limits invitations to two partners, choose the allow list.

concepts.heading: SSPR Scope, Methods, and Registration
concepts.body: Self-service password reset is enabled under Password reset, Properties for None, Selected or All users. Selected accepts one group, but nested groups are supported, so put several team groups inside one parent group and select it. SSPR needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 or a Microsoft 365 plan that includes it for the users who use it. You choose the allowed methods, such as the Microsoft Authenticator app, a mobile phone or an email address, and whether one or two are required. Raising the requirement from one to two blocks users who registered only one method until they add another. To make users register before they need a reset, set Require users to register when signing in to Yes and choose how many days pass before they reconfirm their details. Administrator accounts get a separate default policy you cannot change, normally a two-gate policy that requires two methods.

concepts.heading: Password Writeback for Synchronized Users
concepts.body: When users are synchronized from on-premises Active Directory Domain Services with Microsoft Entra Connect, their password is mastered on premises. Without writeback, a synchronized user who tries SSPR is told to contact the administrator. Password writeback sends a reset or changed password back to AD DS in real time, where the on-premises password policy is checked. It works with password hash synchronization, pass-through authentication and federation, so no sign-in method change is needed. You turn it on in two places: the Password writeback optional feature in the Microsoft Entra Connect wizard, and Write back passwords to your on-premises directory under Password reset, On-premises integration. Traffic is outbound only over port 443 through a relay, so no inbound firewall rule is needed. Writeback requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium; Business Standard includes cloud-only SSPR.

examPoints: A question in which members of a nested group receive no license, or a user loses email while moving between licensed groups, is testing how group-based licensing applies to direct members only and processes changes in the background.
A question that limits who may invite guests or which domains may be invited is testing the separate Guest invite settings, Guest Inviter role and Collaboration restrictions allow or deny list.

A question in which synchronized users cannot reset their passwords while cloud-only users can is testing password writeback, which must be enabled both in Microsoft Entra Connect and in the SSPR on-premises integration settings.

quiz.q: Microsoft 365 E3 is assigned to the group LIC-Staff. Users who are members of LIC-Staff only through the nested group Team-Ops show no E3 license and no error. What should the administrator do?
choices: Assign E3 to Team-Ops as well, or add its users directly to LIC-Staff, because group licenses reach direct members only
Select Reprocess on LIC-Staff, because nested members are processed only after an administrator retries the assignment
Set a usage location on each Team-Ops user, because nested members without one are skipped silently by group licensing
Convert Team-Ops to dynamic membership, because only dynamic nested groups are expanded by group-based licensing
quiz.explain: Group-based licensing does not follow nested groups, so the Team-Ops users were never in scope and no error appears. Choice C is tempting because a missing usage location is a common licensing cause, but group licensing uses the tenant's location for such users and would not silently skip them.

quiz.q: A company is enabling password writeback for SSPR. The network team asks which firewall change the Microsoft Entra Connect server needs for writeback to work. What should the administrator answer?
choices: An inbound rule for TCP 443 on the Microsoft Entra Connect server, so the cloud service can deliver reset requests to it
An inbound rule for TCP 445 on the domain controllers, so the cloud service can write the new password into AD DS directly
No inbound rule, because writeback uses outbound connections over port 443 through a relay to receive the reset requests
A site-to-site VPN between the datacenter and Azure, because writeback traffic is never allowed to cross the public internet
quiz.explain: Password writeback communicates outbound over port 443 through a relay, so no inbound rule is required. Choice A is the classic distractor: it assumes the cloud connects in to the server, but the connection is always started from the Microsoft Entra Connect server.

days.recap: Group-based licensing reaches only direct members and reports errors you fix by freeing licenses or plans and reprocessing; B2B settings control who invites and which domains, and SSPR needs a scope, registered methods and, for synchronized users, password writeback.

days.title: Azure RBAC Roles: Control Plane, Data Plane, and Built-In Roles

concepts.heading: How a Role Assignment Works
concepts.body: Azure role-based access control answers who can do what, where. A role assignment joins three things: a security principal (a user, group, service principal or managed identity), a role definition, and a scope. A role definition lists permitted operations in Actions and data operations in DataActions, plus NotActions and NotDataActions that trim those lists, and AssignableScopes that say where the role can be used. Effective access is the sum of all assignments that apply to the principal; there is no most-specific-wins rule. NotActions is not a deny: it only removes operations from that one role, so if a second role grants the operation, the user can perform it. For example, Contributor plus User Access Administrator on one storage account lets a user assign roles on that account. Only a deny assignment blocks an operation that a role grants.

concepts.heading: Control Plane and Data Plane
concepts.body: Azure separates managing a resource, the control plane handled by Azure Resource Manager, from working with the data inside it, the data plane. Owner has Actions set to the wildcard * (every operation) but no DataActions, so on its own it cannot read blobs with a Microsoft Entra sign-in; it usually reaches data only by listing the account keys. Storage Blob Data Reader, Contributor and Owner grant blob DataActions, and to browse blobs in the portal a user also needs at least Reader on the storage account so the portal can find it. Key Vault follows the same split: Key Vault Contributor manages vaults but cannot read secrets, while Key Vault Secrets User reads secret values in a vault that uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Signing in to a VM with Microsoft Entra ID needs Virtual Machine User Login or Virtual Machine Administrator Login, which Owner and Contributor do not include.

concepts.heading: Owner, Contributor, Reader, and the Access Roles
concepts.body: Four roles appear in almost every exam scenario. Owner has full access to resources and can assign roles. Contributor can create and manage every resource, but its NotActions exclude Microsoft.Authorization write and delete operations, so it cannot assign roles, create or remove resource locks, or create policy assignments. Reader can view resources and their settings but change nothing. User Access Administrator can manage all of Microsoft.Authorization and read resources, without changing them. A newer role, Role Based Access Control Administrator, can only create and delete role assignments and read resources. When you assign it you can add a condition that limits which roles it may hand out and to which principals, for example only Backup Contributor and Backup Reader to the Marketing group. That conditional delegation is Microsoft's recommended least-privilege way to let someone manage access without making them an Owner.

concepts.heading: Service-Specific Built-In Roles
concepts.body: Most daily administration uses narrower built-in roles scoped to one service. Virtual Machine Contributor manages VMs but not the virtual network or storage account they connect to. Network Contributor manages networking resources. Storage Account Contributor manages storage accounts and can list the account keys, and Reader and Data Access can view everything and list keys too, and a key gives full data access through Shared Key outside Azure RBAC. Website Contributor manages web apps, Backup Contributor manages backups but cannot grant access, and Tag Contributor manages tags without access to the resources themselves. The exam rewards picking the narrowest role that does the job at the narrowest scope. If a scenario says the person must restart and resize VMs but must not change networking or assign roles, Virtual Machine Contributor at the resource group is the answer, not Contributor.

concepts.heading: Custom Roles
concepts.body: When no built-in role fits, you can create a custom role. It is a JSON definition with a name, a description, Actions, NotActions, DataActions, NotDataActions and AssignableScopes, created in the portal by cloning a role, or with az role definition create or New-AzRoleDefinition. AssignableScopes lists the management groups, subscriptions or resource groups where the role can be assigned. A typical example is a Lock Manager role with Actions of Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* and the read-everything wildcard */read, which lets a team manage resource locks without the power to grant roles. Wildcards are allowed, such as Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/*, and NotActions can remove a single operation from that set. Remember the same rules as for built-in roles: NotActions only trims this role, and a user who also holds Contributor still gets everything Contributor grants. Custom roles are tied to the directory and are deleted if the subscription moves to another tenant.

examPoints: A question in which an Owner or Contributor cannot read blobs, read secrets or sign in to a VM is testing the split between control plane Actions and data plane DataActions.

A question that asks who can assign roles but must not manage resources is testing User Access Administrator and Role Based Access Control Administrator, the latter with a condition for least privilege.
A question in which a role's NotActions seem to be ignored is testing that NotActions only trims one role and that permissions from all assignments add up.

quiz.q: An operations engineer must start, stop, resize and reconfigure the VMs in rg-vm. She must not change virtual networks or assign roles to anyone. Which built-in role should be assigned at rg-vm?
choices: Contributor, because restarting and resizing a VM needs write access to every resource type that is inside the resource group
Owner on each VM, because only Owner includes the power operations together with resizing and changes to the VM settings
Virtual Machine Contributor, because it manages virtual machines without access to the virtual network they connect to
Network Contributor, because resizing a VM changes its network interface and that change is authorized by the network role
quiz.explain: Virtual Machine Contributor manages VMs but not the virtual network or storage they connect to, and it cannot assign roles. Choice A would work technically, but Contributor could also change the virtual networks in rg-vm, which breaks the requirement.

quiz.q: A user holds a custom role at rg-app whose Actions include Microsoft.Compute/* and whose NotActions include Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete. She is also assigned Contributor at the same scope. Can she delete a VM in rg-app?
choices: No, because the NotActions entry in the custom role acts as a deny that blocks the operation for every role she holds there
Yes, because Contributor grants the delete operation and NotActions only removes it from the custom role, not from other roles
No, because when two roles apply at one scope Azure uses the role that was assigned first, which here is the custom role
Yes, but only after an Owner approves the request, because conflicting role assignments send every delete to an approver
quiz.explain: Effective permissions are the union of all assignments, and NotActions only trims the role it appears in, so Contributor still grants the delete. Choice A describes a deny assignment, which is a different object that Azure creates for features such as deployment stacks.

days.recap: A role assignment joins a principal, a role definition and a scope; permissions from all assignments add up, control plane roles do not grant data access, and the narrowest built-in or custom role at the narrowest scope is the exam's answer.

days.title: Role Scopes, Inheritance, and Interpreting Access

concepts.heading: Scopes and Inheritance
concepts.body: Azure roles can be assigned at four levels: management group, subscription, resource group and resource, and for some services even a child resource such as a single blob container. An assignment applies to its scope and everything below it, never upward or sideways. Reader at a subscription plus Contributor on rg-dev means Contributor in rg-dev and Reader everywhere else. Because a role assignment stores its scope as a resource ID, moving a resource to another resource group gives it a new ID and leaves any assignment made directly on it behind, so you re-create it after the move. Inherited assignments from the subscription still apply if the resource stays in the same subscription. Moving a subscription to another Microsoft Entra directory deletes all its role assignments and custom roles. Exam scenarios reward the narrowest scope that works, for example a data role on one container rather than the account.

concepts.heading: Check Access and Listing Assignments
concepts.body: Access control (IAM) has a Check access tab where you pick any user, group, service principal or managed identity and see its role assignments and deny assignments at that scope. It shows assignments at the scope you opened and those inherited from parents, but not assignments made on child scopes. So checking a user at the subscription can show nothing even though the user is Contributor on a resource group; open the resource group instead. From the command line, az role assignment list --all --assignee user@contoso.com lists assignments across the subscription, and --include-inherited adds parent scopes. A new assignment can take up to about ten minutes to take effect because Azure Resource Manager caches data; signing out and in again, or getting a new token, picks it up sooner. Group changes for managed identities can take much longer because of token caching.

concepts.heading: Deny Assignments
concepts.body: A deny assignment blocks specific actions for specific principals at a scope, even when a role assignment grants them, and Azure evaluates it before role assignments. Unlike role assignments, you cannot create deny assignments directly. Azure creates and manages them for features such as deployment stacks with deny settings and Azure managed applications. A deployment stack set to DenyDelete or DenyWriteAndDelete protects its managed resources from everyone, including Owners, unless a principal is listed in the excluded principals. The deny assignments appear on the Deny assignments tab of Access control (IAM) with the denied and excluded principals. To lift one, change its source: update the deployment stack's deny settings or add the person to its exclusions. Adding another role assignment, even Owner, never outweighs a deny assignment. When a question shows an Owner who is blocked and the portal lists a deny assignment, think of the stack.

concepts.heading: Azure Roles Versus Microsoft Entra Roles
concepts.body: Azure has two separate role systems. Azure roles, such as Owner, Contributor and Virtual Machine Contributor, manage Azure resources and are scoped to management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources. Microsoft Entra roles, such as Global Administrator, User Administrator, Groups Administrator and Guest Inviter, manage directory objects like users, groups, licenses and app registrations. Users do not live inside a subscription, so a role that resets passwords can never be scoped to a resource group. Microsoft Entra roles are scoped to the whole tenant, to an administrative unit, or to a single object. An administrative unit is a container of users, groups or devices, so a help desk lead can be User Administrator only for the Busan office users. By default a Global Administrator has no access to Azure resources at all, which surprises many candidates.

concepts.heading: Elevating Access
concepts.body: Because Global Administrators have no Azure resource access by default, Microsoft provides a documented bridge. In Microsoft Entra ID, Properties, a Global Administrator can set Access management for Azure resources to Yes. This assigns that user the User Access Administrator role at root scope, shown as /, which covers every management group and subscription in the tenant. It is the way to recover a subscription whose only Owner has left, or to make the first role assignment on the tenant root management group, which starts with no assignments. After signing in again, the administrator assigns the roles that are needed, for example Owner on the subscription for a new lead. The elevation does not expire on its own. Remove it by setting the toggle back to No as the same user, or with PowerShell, the CLI or the REST API.

examPoints: A question in which Check access shows nothing for a user who clearly has access is testing that Check access lists the current scope and its parents but never child scopes.
A question in which an Owner is blocked and the portal lists a deny assignment is testing deny assignments created by deployment stacks, which are lifted by changing the stack, not by adding roles.

A question that asks where to scope a password reset or group management role is testing that Microsoft Entra roles use the tenant, administrative units or single objects, never Azure resource scopes.

quiz.q: Lee has Reader at the subscription and Contributor on the resource group rg-dev in that subscription. What can Lee do?
choices: Only read resources everywhere, because a role at the parent scope overrides any role assigned on a resource group below it
Create and change resources anywhere in the subscription, because Contributor on one group spreads up to its subscription
Only read resources everywhere, because when two roles apply Azure always enforces the most restrictive of the two roles
Create and change resources in rg-dev and only read resources elsewhere, because role assignments add up at each scope
quiz.explain: Assignments apply downward and add up, so rg-dev gets Reader plus Contributor while other groups get only Reader. Choice B is wrong because inheritance never flows upward from a resource group to its subscription.

quiz.q: A marketing coordinator must manage membership of the marketing groups only, and nothing else in the directory. Where should the Groups Administrator role be assigned?
choices: To an administrative unit that contains the marketing groups, because Microsoft Entra roles can be scoped to administrative units
At the subscription that hosts the marketing resources, because the subscription scope limits the role to marketing objects
At the management group of the marketing subscriptions, because management groups scope roles for groups of directory objects
At the resource group that holds the marketing resources, because group objects are stored beside the resources they protect
quiz.explain: Groups Administrator is a Microsoft Entra role, and an administrative unit limits it to the groups placed inside. Choice B mixes up the two role systems: subscriptions scope Azure roles for resources, and groups are directory objects that do not live in any subscription.

days.recap: Azure roles inherit downward from management groups to resources and add up, Check access ignores child scopes, deny assignments come from features like deployment stacks, and Microsoft Entra roles use the tenant, administrative units or objects, with elevation as the bridge to Azure.

days.title: Azure Policy and Resource Locks

concepts.heading: Definitions, Initiatives, Assignments, and Parameters
concepts.body: A policy definition holds a rule and an effect, for example Allowed locations with the effect Deny. An initiative groups several definitions so they are assigned and tracked as one unit. An assignment applies a definition or an initiative to a scope, which can be a management group, subscription, resource group or resource, and supplies parameter values. Parameters make one definition reusable: an initiative can declare an allowed-locations parameter and pass it to every member definition, then be assigned to the EU and US management groups with different region lists. If you add a parameter to a definition that is already assigned, it needs a defaultValue so existing assignments stay valid, and parameters cannot be removed. Watch the built-ins: Allowed locations excludes resource groups, so pair it with Allowed locations for resource groups. Writing assignments needs Owner or Resource Policy Contributor, because Contributor can only read them.

concepts.heading: Effects and Enforcement Mode
concepts.body: The effect decides what a policy does. Deny blocks a non-compliant create or update request. Audit only records non-compliance, and AuditIfNotExists checks for a related resource such as a diagnostic setting. Modify adds, replaces or removes properties such as tags, Append adds fields, and DeployIfNotExists deploys a missing related resource. DenyAction blocks specific actions such as deletion, Disabled turns a definition off, and Manual records an attestation. Most effects act on create and update requests (DenyAction on delete requests); for existing resources a compliance scan only marks them non-compliant. Every assignment also has an enforcement mode. With DoNotEnforce, shown in the portal as Disabled, the effect is not applied to requests but resources are still evaluated and reported, which lets you preview a Deny-only policy safely before switching enforcement back on. An on-demand scan, az policy state trigger-scan, refreshes compliance results without changing any resources.

concepts.heading: Remediation and Managed Identities
concepts.body: Modify and DeployIfNotExists change resources, and Azure Policy does that with a managed identity attached to the assignment, not with the account of the administrator. The definition lists the roles that identity needs in roleDefinitionIds. When you assign the policy in the portal, Azure Policy creates the identity and grants those roles automatically; when you assign it with Azure CLI, PowerShell or an SDK, the identity is created but you must grant the roles yourself, otherwise every deployment fails with an authorization error. New and updated resources are fixed as their requests pass through. Existing non-compliant resources are fixed only by a remediation task, started from the assignment. For example, after Finance changes the CostCenter tag on a resource group, an Inherit a tag from the resource group assignment needs a new remediation task before older resources show the new value. Granting roles to that identity requires User Access Administrator or Owner.

concepts.heading: Exclusions and Exemptions
concepts.body: There are two ways to keep a policy away from part of its scope. An exclusion, the notScopes list on the assignment, removes child scopes or resources from evaluation entirely: they are not evaluated by any definition in an initiative and disappear from compliance counts. Use it for broad, permanent cases, such as a sandbox subscription that does not need production rules. An exemption is a separate object created on a resource or scope. The resource shows as Exempt in compliance reports, so it stays visible. An exemption has a category, Waiver when non-compliance is temporarily accepted or Mitigated when the intent is met another way, can be limited to selected definitions of an initiative through their reference IDs, and can carry an expiresOn date after which it is no longer honored. For a legacy storage account that breaks one rule until it is retired in 90 days, choose a Waiver exemption with an expiry date.

concepts.heading: Lock Levels and Who Manages Them
concepts.body: Resource locks protect resources from accidental change regardless of anyone's role. CanNotDelete, shown as Delete in the portal, lets authorized users read and modify a resource but not delete it. ReadOnly lets users read a resource but not delete or change it, which is like giving everyone, Owners included, Reader for control plane operations. Locks can be applied to a subscription, a resource group or a single resource, and child resources inherit them; management groups cannot be locked. When locks overlap, the more restrictive one applies. Locks are Microsoft.Authorization/locks resources, so creating or deleting them needs Owner, User Access Administrator or a custom role with Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*. Contributor cannot create locks because its NotActions exclude Microsoft.Authorization writes. Locks override role permissions: an Owner who wants to delete a locked resource must remove the lock first, for example with az lock delete, and then delete the resource.

concepts.heading: Lock Side Effects
concepts.body: Locks act on control plane requests to Azure Resource Manager, which has surprising results. A ReadOnly lock blocks every POST operation, so listing storage account keys, starting or restarting a VM, and scaling an App Service plan up or out all fail, even for Owners. Data plane traffic is not affected, so a user with a blob data role can still upload blobs with a Microsoft Entra sign-in. A CanNotDelete lock on a resource group also blocks the automatic clean-up of deployment history, so frequent deployments eventually reach the history limit and fail, and on the group used by Azure Backup it blocks restore point clean-up. A CanNotDelete lock on any one resource makes deletion of its whole resource group fail, with nothing deleted at all. Use CanNotDelete when the goal is only to stop deletion, place locks on critical resources rather than whole groups where clean-up matters, and keep ReadOnly for truly frozen resources.

examPoints: A question in which existing resources stay non-compliant after a Modify or DeployIfNotExists assignment, or remediation fails with an authorization error, is testing remediation tasks and the roles granted to the assignment's managed identity.
A question that wants a time-limited, still-reported exception for one resource is testing a Waiver exemption with an expiry date, while a permanent carve-out of a whole scope is an exclusion.
A question in which an Owner cannot restart a VM, list storage keys or delete a resource group is testing ReadOnly or CanNotDelete lock side effects, which override every role.

quiz.q: An administrator places a ReadOnly lock on rg-data to stop configuration drift. The next day an Owner of the group cannot restart a VM in rg-data, and the portal cannot list the storage account keys. What explains both failures?
choices: Adding the lock removed the role assignments in the group, so the Owner now holds only the Reader role for every resource
A ReadOnly lock blocks every POST request, such as restarting a VM or listing keys, for all users including the Owners
The lock applies only to resources created after it, so the failures come from a separate deny assignment on the group
A ReadOnly lock takes up to 24 hours to settle, and during that time all operations on the group are refused for safety
quiz.explain: Restarting a VM and listing storage keys are POST operations, which a ReadOnly lock blocks for everyone whatever their role. Choice A is wrong because locks never change role assignments; the Owner keeps the role, and the lock simply overrides it.

quiz.q: Security wants every key vault, existing and future, to send its logs to a central Log Analytics workspace through a diagnostic setting. Which policy approach meets the requirement?
choices: An Audit policy assigned at the subscription, which reports vaults without a diagnostic setting and adds one at the next scan
An Append policy assigned at the subscription, which appends a diagnostic setting to every vault the next time anyone reads it
A DeployIfNotExists policy with a managed identity, plus a remediation task that deploys the setting on vaults that already exist
A Deny policy assigned at the subscription, which blocks new vaults and rebuilds existing vaults with a diagnostic setting added
quiz.explain: DeployIfNotExists deploys the missing diagnostic setting through the assignment's managed identity, and a remediation task fixes the vaults that already exist. Choice A only reports non-compliance; Audit never changes a resource, however many scans run.

days.recap: Azure Policy assigns parameterized definitions and initiatives whose effects act on requests, with remediation tasks and a managed identity for existing resources and exemptions for tracked exceptions, while CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks block control plane changes for every role.

days.title: Tags, Resource Groups, Subscriptions, Management Groups, and Cost Control

concepts.heading: Tags and Tag Inheritance
concepts.body: A tag is a name and value pair, such as CostCenter = 4410, on a resource, resource group or subscription. Tag names are case-insensitive for operations, but values are case-sensitive, so Production and production split a cost report into two lines. Each object holds up to 50 tag pairs, and tags are plain text, so never store secrets in them. Tags are not inherited: a tag on a resource group is not copied to the resources inside. To make resources follow the group, assign the built-in policy Inherit a tag from the resource group, which uses the Modify effect, and run a remediation task for existing resources. The Tag Contributor role manages tags without access to the resources, through PowerShell or the REST API. In PowerShell, Update-AzTag with -Operation Merge adds or changes tags and keeps the others, while New-AzTag replaces the whole set.

concepts.heading: Resource Groups and Moving Resources
concepts.body: A resource group is a logical container whose location only stores its metadata; its resources can sit in other regions. Deleting a group deletes everything in it, and the only permission needed is the delete action on the resource group, which overrides delete actions listed in NotActions for the resources inside. Resources can be moved to another resource group or subscription without changing their region. Before a cross-subscription move, check that both subscriptions are in the same Microsoft Entra tenant, that the resource type supports moves, that the destination subscription is registered for the resource provider, for example with az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Batch, and that it has enough quota. Dependent resources must move together. Role assignments made directly on a moved resource stay behind and must be re-created at the new scope, because the resource gets a new resource ID.

concepts.heading: Subscriptions, Transfers, and Quotas
concepts.body: A subscription is a billing and management boundary that trusts exactly one Microsoft Entra directory. Transferring a subscription to another directory keeps the resources and the subscription ID, but it permanently deletes role assignments and custom roles, drops Azure Policy definitions, assignments and exemptions, and breaks managed identities. Export assignments first with az role assignment list --all, then re-create them; disable and re-enable system-assigned identities and re-create user-assigned ones. Billing ownership transfer is a different operation that changes who pays. Subscriptions also carry quotas: virtual machines are limited by a total regional vCPU quota and a per-family quota, such as D-series vCPUs in West Europe. When a size is listed under Insufficient quota - family limit, request an increase on the Quotas page or from the Request quota link. Moving VMs to another resource group never helps, because quotas count per subscription and region.

concepts.heading: Management Group Hierarchy
concepts.body: Management groups organize subscriptions so that policies and role assignments made at a group apply to every subscription below it. Each tenant has one root management group, the Tenant root group, whose ID is the tenant ID; it cannot be moved or deleted and starts with no role assignments, so a Global Administrator must elevate access before managing it. The tree supports up to six levels below the root, not counting the subscription level, and each subscription has exactly one parent. Hierarchy settings on the root let you choose a default management group, such as Sandbox, where new subscriptions land instead of the root, and require authorization before anyone can create management groups; changing them needs the Hierarchy Settings Administrator role or equivalent. A management group can be deleted only when it has no child groups or subscriptions and you have write permission on it, and it can never carry a resource lock.

concepts.heading: Budgets and Cost Alerts
concepts.body: Microsoft Cost Management budgets track spending against an amount for a monthly, quarterly or annual period and send alerts at thresholds you choose, based on actual cost or forecasted cost. Budgets can be created at management group, subscription, resource group and billing scopes, and a budget never stops resources by itself. To act on a threshold, a budget calls an action group that can run an automation runbook, call a webhook or send a notification, but action groups are supported only for budgets at subscription and resource group scope. Cost data typically arrives within 8 to 24 hours and budgets are evaluated every 24 hours, so alerts are not instant. Other cost alerts include credit, department spending quota and anomaly alerts. Group costs by tag in Cost analysis to charge back departments. A question that wants a budget to stop VMs automatically needs a subscription or resource group budget with an action group.

concepts.heading: Azure Advisor Recommendations
concepts.body: Azure Advisor reviews your resources and gives recommendations in five categories: reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence. Cost recommendations include shutting down VMs that are barely used and resizing VMs whose load fits a cheaper size. These are based on utilization over a lookback period that defaults to seven days, which can mislead for workloads that peak once a month, such as a payroll batch. In the Advisor configuration you can change the VM lookback period to 14, 21, 30, 60 or 90 days, and recommendations update within about two days. You can also exclude subscriptions or resource groups from Advisor, and dismiss or postpone a single recommendation that does not apply. The estimated savings use retail rates, so real savings can be lower. When a scenario says Advisor keeps recommending shutdown of a VM that runs at month end, lengthen the lookback period.

examPoints: A question in which resources do not show a tag that was added to their resource group is testing that tags are not inherited and that a Modify policy with a remediation task copies them.
A question about a failed cross-subscription move, lost access after a move, or a subscription moved to another directory is testing move prerequisites and what a directory transfer deletes.

A question that wants new subscriptions kept away from root-level policies, or a budget that triggers automation, is testing the default management group setting and the subscription or resource group scope rule for budget action groups.

quiz.q: An administrator moves the storage account stlogs from rg-a to rg-b in the same subscription. A group had Storage Blob Data Contributor assigned directly on stlogs. What must she do after the move?
choices: Re-create the group's role assignment on stlogs, because assignments made directly on a resource do not move with it
Move the storage account back to its original region, because moving between resource groups also moves the region
Re-enter every tag on the account, because a move between resource groups clears the tags that were set on the resource
Nothing at all, because every role assignment, tag and setting moves together with the resource to the new group
quiz.explain: A direct role assignment stores the old resource ID and is left behind, so it must be re-created on the moved account. Choice B is wrong because a move changes only the resource group or subscription, never the region.

quiz.q: Finance wants every resource in a subscription to carry its resource group's CostCenter tag, including the hundreds of resources that already exist. What should the administrator do?
choices: Add the CostCenter tag to each resource group, because resources copy the tags of their group on the next daily scan
Create a budget filtered on CostCenter, because budgets apply the tag of their scope to every resource they include
Place a ReadOnly lock on each resource group, because locked groups pass their tags down to the resources they hold
Assign the Inherit a tag from the resource group policy and run a remediation task for the resources that already exist
quiz.explain: Tags are not inherited on their own; the built-in Modify policy copies the group tag on create and update, and a remediation task fixes existing resources. Choice A describes inheritance that Azure does not do, so the tags would stay only on the groups.

days.recap: Tags are case-sensitive in value and not inherited without policy, resources move between groups and subscriptions under clear prerequisites, management groups arrange subscriptions under one root, and budgets alert, with action groups only at subscription and resource group scope.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Identities and Governance

concepts.heading: Identity Objects Recap
concepts.body: Days 1 and 2 covered the objects in Microsoft Entra ID. User type, Member or Guest, sets directory permissions independently of where the user signs in. Security groups grant access and can hold devices, Microsoft 365 groups add a mailbox, calendar and site and hold only users, and the group type is fixed at creation while the membership type can change. Dynamic groups take members only from their rule, where -and is evaluated before -or. Bulk create makes members with passwords and no email, Bulk invite makes guests who get invitations, and deleted users come back with the same object ID for 30 days. Group-based licensing reaches direct members only, falls back to the tenant usage location, and reports errors such as not enough licenses or conflicting service plans that you fix and then reprocess. If you can explain each of these in one sentence, the identity questions become quick.

concepts.heading: External Access and SSPR Recap
concepts.body: External collaboration settings split three jobs: Guest user access limits what guests see, Guest invite settings and the Guest Inviter role decide who may invite, and Collaboration restrictions decide which domains, with an allow list for named partners or a deny list for blocked domains. Lists stop new and pending invitations but leave redeemed guests in place. Self-service password reset is scoped to None, Selected or All, where Selected takes one group that may contain nested groups. Users must have registered at least as many methods as the policy requires, so require registration at sign-in and set a reconfirmation interval. Synchronized users need password writeback, switched on in Microsoft Entra Connect and in the SSPR on-premises integration page, using outbound connections only. Licensing is part of the answer here: P1 or a Microsoft 365 plan with SSPR for SSPR users, P1 or Business Premium for writeback, and P1 for members of dynamic groups.

concepts.heading: Access Control Recap
concepts.body: Days 3 and 4 covered Azure RBAC. A role assignment is a principal, a role and a scope; permissions from all assignments add up, NotActions only trims one role, and only deny assignments, created by Azure for features such as deployment stacks, block granted actions. Control plane roles like Owner and Contributor carry no DataActions, so reading blobs, reading secrets or signing in to a VM needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader, Key Vault Secrets User or Virtual Machine User Login. Contributor cannot write anything under Microsoft.Authorization, so it cannot assign roles, create locks or assign policies. Role Based Access Control Administrator with a condition is the least-privilege way to delegate access management. Assignments inherit downward only, Check access ignores child scopes, and Microsoft Entra roles use tenant, administrative unit or object scopes, while elevation gives a Global Administrator User Access Administrator at root.

concepts.heading: Governance Tools Side by Side
concepts.body: Many Domain 1 questions list several governance tools as choices, so know their jobs. Azure RBAC decides who can perform an action. Azure Policy decides what may exist and how it must be configured, for everyone, with effects such as Deny, Audit, Modify and DeployIfNotExists; DoNotEnforce previews a policy, remediation tasks fix existing resources, exclusions remove scopes and exemptions record tracked exceptions. Resource locks stop deletion or change even by Owners, with side effects on POST operations, deployment history and resource group deletion. Tags label resources for cost and organization but grant nothing. Management groups arrange subscriptions so that policies and roles flow down, and their hierarchy settings decide where new subscriptions land. Budgets watch spending and alert, and Advisor recommends. Read the requirement's verb: prevent creation is Policy, prevent deletion is a lock, allow an action is RBAC.

concepts.heading: Subscriptions, Moves, and Cost Recap
concepts.body: Day 6 tied governance to day-to-day administration. Moving resources keeps their region, needs the same tenant and a registered resource provider in the destination, and leaves direct role assignments behind. Moving a subscription between management groups needs write access on both parents, and an Owner role inherited from the current parent allows a move only to a group where you are also Owner. Transferring a subscription to another directory keeps resources and the subscription ID but deletes role assignments and custom roles, drops policy objects and breaks managed identities. vCPU quotas are per subscription, region and VM family and are raised through Quotas. Budgets alert on actual or forecasted cost and call action groups only at subscription and resource group scope. Advisor's VM lookback period can be lengthened for monthly workloads. Revisit any of these in which your error log shows two or more misses.

examPoints: A question that lists Azure RBAC, Azure Policy and a resource lock as choices is testing whether the requirement is about who can act, what may exist, or what must not be deleted or changed.

A question in which an administrator with a powerful role still fails is testing one of the Domain 1 limits: no DataActions, no Microsoft.Authorization writes for Contributor, a lock, a deny assignment, or a Microsoft Entra role used where an Azure role is needed.

A question that adds a scope or timing detail, such as existing resources versus new ones, or a child scope versus its parent, is testing remediation tasks and inheritance, the two ideas that decide most Domain 1 items worth 20 to 25 percent of the exam.

quiz.q: A production SQL server must never be deleted by accident, even by subscription Owners, but administrators must still be able to change its settings. What should be configured?
choices: An Azure Policy assignment with the Deny effect on the server, which blocks delete requests from every principal in the scope
The Reader role for all administrators on the server's resource group, so that they can view the server but never delete it
A CanNotDelete lock on the server, which blocks deletion for every role while still allowing changes to its configuration
A ReadOnly lock on the server, which blocks deletion for every role while still allowing changes to its configuration
quiz.explain: A CanNotDelete lock stops deletion regardless of role and still allows updates. Choice D is tempting because it also stops deletion, but ReadOnly blocks configuration changes too, which the administrators still need.

quiz.q: Compliance requires that only VM sizes from an approved list can be created in the Sub-Prod subscription, whoever deploys them. What should the administrator use?
choices: An assignment of the built-in policy Allowed virtual machine size SKUs at Sub-Prod, with the approved sizes as its parameter
A custom Azure role for all deployers at Sub-Prod whose NotActions remove the create action for every unapproved VM size
A monthly budget at Sub-Prod with an action group that deletes any VM whose size is not on the approved list of sizes
A CanNotDelete lock at Sub-Prod, which stops deployers from creating VMs unless their size is listed on the lock itself
quiz.explain: Azure Policy controls what may be created for everyone, and this built-in definition takes the allowed sizes as a parameter. Choice B confuses RBAC with Policy: role definitions grant operations by resource type, not by property values such as a VM size.

days.recap: Domain 1 is identities in Microsoft Entra ID, access through Azure RBAC, and governance through Azure Policy, locks, tags, management groups and cost tools; match each requirement's verb to the tool that does exactly that job.

days.title: Securing Access to Storage: Firewalls, SAS, Keys, and Identity-Based Access

concepts.heading: Storage Firewall and Network Rules
concepts.body: When public network access is set to Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, only allowed sources reach the account's public endpoint and everything else gets a 403 error. Virtual network rules allow a subnet that has a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage, or Microsoft.Storage.Global for any region. IP network rules allow public IPv4 addresses or ranges, such as the public address of an office firewall; private ranges like 192.168.40.0/24 are rejected, and /31 and /32 prefixes are not supported, so enter a single address instead. Requests from the same Azure region as the account use private Azure addresses, so IP rules never match them and same-region VMs need a virtual network rule. The firewall filters only data plane requests: an administrator outside the allowed network can still list containers in the portal through the control plane, but browsing blobs fails.

concepts.heading: Trusted Services and Resource Instance Rules
concepts.body: Some Azure services do not run in your virtual network, so two exceptions exist. The trusted services exception, shown in the portal as Allow Azure services on the trusted services list to access this storage account and set with --bypass AzureServices, admits listed services such as Azure Monitor, Azure Backup, Azure Site Recovery and Azure File Sync. This is how a diagnostic setting writes Microsoft Entra sign-in logs to a firewalled account. A resource instance rule admits one specific resource, such as an Azure AI Search service or a Data Factory, from the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Network access is not data access: the resource's managed identity still needs a data role, for example Storage Blob Data Reader, to read blobs. The Logging and Metrics bypass values only let services read log files and metrics tables in your account, and they do not admit Azure Monitor's writes.

concepts.heading: Shared Access Signatures
concepts.body: A shared access signature is a token in a URL that delegates limited access. A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key that a Microsoft Entra principal obtains, so it traces back to an identity, lasts at most seven days, and is Microsoft's recommended kind; creating one needs a role with generateUserDelegationKey, such as Storage Blob Data Contributor, and az storage container generate-sas --auth-mode login --as-user. A service SAS is signed with an account key and covers one resource in one service. An account SAS is also key-signed and adds several services in one token and service-level operations such as Get Service Properties, chosen with ss, for example ss=bq, and srt=s. Any SAS can carry sip, a client IP address or range, and spr=https; the default protocol setting allows both HTTPS and HTTP. A SAS IP limit narrows the token and never opens the storage firewall.

concepts.heading: Stored Access Policies and Revoking SAS
concepts.body: A stored access policy lives on a container, file share, queue or table, holds a start time, expiry and permissions, and is referenced by a service SAS through its identifier; each container can hold up to five. Only a service SAS can use one. Its advantage is control after issue: change the policy's expiry to extend or shorten every SAS that uses it, or delete, rename or expire it to revoke them all, without touching the account keys. An ad hoc account or service SAS is revoked only by regenerating the key that signed it. Do it safely: move applications to the other key, confirm they work, then regenerate the leaked key. A user delegation SAS ignores key rotation; revoke it with az storage account revoke-delegation-keys, which invalidates every user delegation SAS on the account, or by removing the role of the principal that created it.

concepts.heading: Access Keys and Shared Key Authorization
concepts.body: Every storage account has two access keys, key1 and key2, and anyone holding one has full access to all data through Shared Key authorization, outside Azure RBAC. Two keys exist so you can rotate without downtime, and regenerating a key revokes every SAS signed with it. Roles that include listKeys, such as Storage Account Contributor and Reader and Data Access, therefore give full data access indirectly. Setting AllowSharedKeyAccess to false makes the account reject key-based requests: connection strings with a key, service SAS and account SAS all fail, while Microsoft Entra requests and user delegation SAS keep working. Before you switch it off, find key users with the Transactions metric split by authentication type or with resource logs. A key expiration policy shows a rotation reminder, but older accounts must rotate both keys once first so the account records each key's creation time. Store keys in Azure Key Vault.

concepts.heading: Identity-Based Access for Azure Files
concepts.body: SMB Azure file shares can authenticate users with Kerberos from one identity source per account. On-premises AD DS needs clients that can reach domain controllers, and the account is joined to the domain. Microsoft Entra Domain Services needs clients joined to the managed domain. Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Microsoft Entra joined or hybrid joined clients authenticate without seeing a domain controller, which suits laptops at home without VPN. Access is then checked in two layers, and the more restrictive wins. Share-level permissions are Azure roles such as Storage File Data SMB Share Reader, SMB Share Contributor and SMB Share Elevated Contributor; directory and file permissions are Windows ACLs. SMB Share Reader with NTFS Full Control still means read only. Identities without a Microsoft Entra counterpart, such as a gMSA or computer account, use a default share-level permission. Mounting with the account key bypasses all of this and grants full access.

examPoints: A question in which an IP rule does not admit Azure VMs, or an Azure service such as Azure Monitor cannot write to a firewalled account, is testing same-region traffic, virtual network rules and the trusted services exception.
A question that requires a SAS with no account key, or asks how to revoke many tokens at once, is testing user delegation SAS, stored access policies and key rotation.

A question in which an Azure Files user can read but not write, or a service account has no Microsoft Entra identity, is testing share-level roles combined with NTFS permissions and the default share-level permission.

quiz.q: An administrator issued 25 service SAS URLs for container reports, all referencing the stored access policy vendor-read, which expires tomorrow. The vendor's contract has been extended by one week. What is the simplest way to keep all 25 URLs working?
choices: Regenerate key1 and issue 25 new service SAS URLs with a new expiry, because a SAS expiry cannot change after it is issued
Issue one account SAS with a one-week expiry for the vendor, because an account SAS replaces existing service SAS tokens
Run az storage account revoke-delegation-keys and then reissue each token, because that renews every SAS on the account
Change the expiry time on the vendor-read stored access policy, because every SAS that references it uses the new value
quiz.explain: A service SAS that references a stored access policy takes its expiry from the policy, so editing the policy updates all 25 URLs at once. Choice A would break the existing URLs and any app that uses key1, which is the opposite of the goal.

quiz.q: An Azure file share uses Microsoft Entra Kerberos. A user has the Storage File Data SMB Share Reader role on the share and NTFS Full Control on the Finance folder. What can she do in Finance?
choices: Take full control of Finance, because NTFS permissions override the share-level role when they grant more access
Only read files, because the more restrictive of the share-level role and the NTFS permissions is the one that applies
Nothing at all, because NTFS permissions are ignored on Azure file shares whenever Microsoft Entra Kerberos is used
Read and write but not delete files, because Azure Files averages the share-level role and the NTFS permission level
quiz.explain: Azure Files applies the more restrictive of the two layers, so the share-level Reader role limits her to read access. Choice A is the common mistake: NTFS permissions can narrow access but never raise it above the share-level role.

days.recap: Storage access combines network rules that filter data plane traffic, trusted service and resource instance exceptions, SAS tokens revoked through stored access policies, key rotation or delegation keys, and for Azure Files a Kerberos identity source with share-level roles plus NTFS permissions.

days.title: Storage Accounts: Types, Redundancy, Replication, and Encryption

concepts.heading: Account Types and Core Settings
concepts.body: Standard general-purpose v2 is the default account type for blobs, files, queues and tables. Three premium types run on solid-state storage: premium block blobs for high transaction rates and low latency, premium file shares, and premium page blobs. The type, including standard versus premium performance, is fixed at creation, so changing it means creating a new account and copying the data. Several security settings matter. Secure transfer required rejects every request made over plain HTTP. Minimum TLS version rejects older TLS; before enforcing TLS 1.2, send resource logs to Log Analytics and query the TlsVersion field to find old clients. Allow Blob anonymous access at the account overrides every container's level. A hierarchical namespace can be enabled on an existing account, but the upgrade is one-way, blocks writes while it runs, and some features, such as object replication, are not supported with it.

concepts.heading: Redundancy Options
concepts.body: Every account keeps several copies of its data. LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter, and ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in the primary region. GRS adds an asynchronous copy in a secondary region using LRS there, and GZRS combines ZRS in the primary with that geo copy. With GRS and GZRS the secondary copy cannot be read until a failover. RA-GRS and RA-GZRS add a read-only secondary endpoint, the account name with -secondary added, such as contosodata-secondary.blob.core.windows.net, that accepts the same keys; the Last Sync Time property shows how far it lags. Azure Files does not support the read-access options. The Archive tier is not supported on ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS accounts. If an app must read data from the secondary region while the primary is down, without a failover, the answer is RA-GRS or RA-GZRS.

concepts.heading: Changing Redundancy and Failover
concepts.body: Redundancy changes come in two kinds. A geo or read-access change, such as LRS to GRS or GRS to RA-GRS, is a simple SKU update in the portal's Redundancy page or with az storage account update --sku. A zone change, such as LRS to ZRS, is a conversion started with az storage account migration start, with no downtime or data loss. LRS to GZRS needs both, done as two separate steps. Archived blobs must leave an account before a zone conversion. For disaster recovery, a customer-managed planned failover swaps regions while both are available, with no data loss expected and geo-redundancy kept, which suits drills. An unplanned failover is for a primary outage: writes after the Last Sync Time can be lost and the account becomes LRS in the new primary until you re-enable geo-redundancy. Plan to start failover yourself: Microsoft-managed failover is reserved for disasters affecting a whole region.

concepts.heading: Object Replication
concepts.body: Object replication copies block blobs asynchronously from a container in a source account to a container in a destination account, which may be in another region. Azure Storage reads the source account's change feed and replays writes and deletes. Prerequisites are blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source; accounts with a hierarchical namespace are not supported, and configuring a policy needs Contributor at the account scope. You create the policy on the destination, then associate the same policy ID with the source, and each rule maps one source container to one destination container, optionally filtered by prefix. By default a new rule copies only blobs created after the rule, so to include older blobs set the copy scope to everything or an earlier creation time. While a rule is active, the destination container rejects writes. Blobs in the Archive tier are not replicated.

concepts.heading: Encryption: Keys, Scopes, and Infrastructure
concepts.body: Azure Storage always encrypts data at rest with 256-bit AES, using Microsoft-managed keys by default. With a customer-managed key, the account's encryption key is wrapped with your RSA key in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM. The vault must have soft delete and purge protection on, and a managed identity needs the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role; at account creation that must be a user-assigned identity, because the account has no system-assigned identity yet. Disabling the key makes reads and writes fail until access returns. Encryption scopes give a container or blob its own key inside one account; a container's default scope, with overrides blocked, keeps each customer's uploads in that customer's key, and disabling a scope cuts off only its data. Infrastructure encryption adds a second encryption layer and can be enabled only when the account is created, so an existing account needs a new account and a data copy.

concepts.heading: Storage Explorer and AzCopy
concepts.body: Azure Storage Explorer is a desktop app for browsing and managing storage data. It connects by signing in with Microsoft Entra ID, with an account name and key, with a SAS URL or connection string, or anonymously to public containers. Microsoft Entra sign-in is the preferred option for someone who has a data role on a container but no management access, because they can attach the container directly. AzCopy is the command-line tool for bulk transfers. After azcopy login, it uses your Microsoft Entra identity, which needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader to download or Storage Blob Data Contributor to upload; an Owner without a data role gets an authorization error, and new assignments can take a few minutes to apply. AzCopy also accepts a SAS on each URL or a VM's managed identity. Copies between accounts run server to server, as in azcopy copy with --recursive.

examPoints: A question that asks to change performance tier or add infrastructure encryption on an existing account is testing settings fixed at creation, which require a new account and a copy.

A question about reading the secondary region without a failover, converting LRS to a zone-redundant option, or a disaster recovery drill is testing RA- options, SKU updates versus conversions, and planned versus unplanned failover.
A question about separate keys per customer in one account, or about missing object replication of older blobs, is testing encryption scopes and the default copy scope of a replication rule.

quiz.q: An auditor has Storage Blob Data Reader on one container and no role on the subscription or storage account. She must browse that container's blobs in Azure Storage Explorer. How should she connect?
choices: Sign in using Microsoft Entra ID and attach the container directly, because her data role is enough for that connection
Use the account name and key, because Storage Explorer cannot attach a single container with a Microsoft Entra sign-in
Ask for Reader at the subscription first, because Storage Explorer must list the subscription before it shows any data
Connect anonymously to the container's URL, because Storage Explorer treats a data role as permission for public access
quiz.explain: Microsoft Entra sign-in is the preferred option when someone has data layer access but no management access, and she can attach the container directly. Choice B would need the account key, which she does not have and which would give far more access than her role.

quiz.q: An administrator changes a Standard general-purpose v2 account from GRS to RA-GRS. What changes for applications?
choices: A third copy of the data is created in another geography, so the account now spans three separate Azure regions
The primary region now stores its copies across availability zones, so a datacenter failure no longer affects writes
A read-only secondary endpoint becomes available, the account name with -secondary added, using the same keys
Automatic failover is turned on, so Azure promotes the secondary region as soon as the primary region becomes slow
quiz.explain: RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary region through the -secondary endpoint, which accepts the same keys. Choice B describes ZRS or GZRS in the primary region, which is a separate zone conversion, not a read-access change.

days.recap: Storage account type, performance and infrastructure encryption are fixed at creation, redundancy ranges from LRS to RA-GZRS with SKU updates for geo changes and conversions for zone changes, and object replication, encryption scopes, Storage Explorer and AzCopy each have prerequisites the exam checks.

days.title: Azure Files and Blob Containers: Protocols, Billing, Access Levels, and Tiers

concepts.heading: SMB and NFS File Shares
concepts.body: Each Azure file share uses one protocol, chosen at creation, and one share cannot be reached with both. SMB shares are mounted by Windows, by Linux with the SMB kernel client, and by macOS, so mixed Windows and Linux clients working on the same files need an SMB share. SMB uses TCP port 445, and clients outside the share's region must use SMB 3.x with encryption. NFS shares, using NFS 4.1, are for Linux workloads that need POSIX permissions, UID and GID ownership and case sensitivity. They are not supported on Windows, need the SSD media tier, and have no user-based authentication: access is decided by the network, through a private endpoint or a service endpoint from an allowed virtual network. IP address firewall rules do not admit NFS clients, so an on-premises Linux server reaches an NFS share through a private endpoint over VPN or ExpressRoute.

concepts.heading: Billing Models and Share Size
concepts.body: Azure Files has three billing models, and Microsoft recommends provisioned v2 for new deployments. With provisioned v2 you provision storage, IOPS and throughput separately and pay for what you provision whether or not it is used. The provisioned storage is a hard limit, so a full share rejects writes until you raise it, and a decrease is allowed only after 24 hours have passed since the last increase. Provisioned v1 sets storage and derives performance from it. Pay-as-you-go bills used storage, transactions and data transfer, exists only on the HDD media tier and supports only SMB. Its size cap is called the quota, and raising the quota does not raise the bill by itself. A share can therefore be full long before its storage account. Share snapshots do not count toward the share's maximum size, so deleting them frees no room.

concepts.heading: Mounting and Connectivity
concepts.body: The portal's Connect page for a share generates a mount script for Windows, Linux or macOS. If it reports that the account is not reachable, test the port with Test-NetConnection to the file endpoint on port 445. Many ISPs and corporate firewalls block outbound 445; the fixes are to open the port or to reach the share privately over a VPN or ExpressRoute, usually through a private endpoint whose private IP on-premises DNS can resolve. SAS tokens are not supported for mounting a share; mounting uses the storage account key or identity-based authentication. Mounting with the key works for testing but gives full control of the share, so production users should use an identity source such as Microsoft Entra Kerberos. A full share stops writes but does not break the TCP connection, so a failed port test points to the network, not to quota.

concepts.heading: Blob Container Anonymous Access Levels
concepts.body: Anonymous read access to blobs needs two settings. At the storage account, Allow Blob anonymous access must be enabled; it is disabled by default for new accounts, and disabling it overrides every container. At the container, the anonymous access level is Private, the default, where every request must be authorized; Blob, where anyone with a blob's URL can read it but nobody can list the container; or Container, where anonymous clients can also list the blobs in it. The level is set per container only, never per blob or virtual folder, because a prefix such as drafts/ is just part of each blob's name. To publish product images while keeping drafts private, keep drafts in a separate Private container and set the public container to Blob. Before disabling anonymous access, find anonymous readers with the Transactions metric filtered on anonymous authentication.

concepts.heading: Access Tiers
concepts.body: Block blobs in a general-purpose v2 account use online tiers hot, cool and cold, or the offline archive tier. Cooler tiers cost less to store but more to read, and they have minimum storage periods: 30 days for cool, 90 for cold and 180 for archive. Deleting, overwriting or re-tiering a blob earlier is charged as early deletion. The account has a default access tier of hot, cool or cold, never archive. A blob uploaded without a tier has an inferred tier that follows the default, shown as Hot (inferred), while a blob whose tier was set explicitly keeps it. Changing the account default re-tiers every inferred blob and is billed as tier change operations, while explicitly tiered blobs stay where they are. For individual blobs use Set Blob Tier, and for rules based on age use lifecycle management. Premium block blob accounts do not use access tiers.

concepts.heading: Rehydrating Archived Blobs
concepts.body: A blob in the archive tier is offline: you can read its metadata, but not its data, and no tool can download it until it is rehydrated to hot, cool or cold. There are two ways. Set Blob Tier changes the tier of the archived blob itself, and Copy Blob copies it to a new blob in an online tier, leaving the archived original in place. Rehydration priority is Standard by default, which can take up to 15 hours for blobs under 10 GB, or High, which may finish in under an hour for such blobs at higher cost. While a Standard request is pending you can raise one urgent blob to High, but you cannot lower High to Standard, and a Set Blob Tier request cannot be cancelled. Snapshots are not supported for archived blobs. Remember that a lifecycle rule can archive a rehydrated blob again, which Day 11 explains.

examPoints: A question that mixes Windows and Linux clients, mounts from a branch office, or tries an IP rule for an NFS share is testing the SMB versus NFS limits and port 445 connectivity.
A question in which a file share is full while the account is not, or that compares paying for usage with paying for capacity, is testing quotas, provisioned size and the three billing models.
A question about public images, inferred tiers, early deletion or an urgent archived blob is testing container access levels, the account default tier and rehydration priority.
