quiz.q: A research team runs a Linux compute cluster that needs POSIX permissions, UID and GID ownership and case-sensitive names on a shared file system. No Windows clients will connect. Which share should the administrator create?
choices: An SMB share on the HDD media tier with pay-as-you-go billing, mounted from Linux with the SMB kernel client on every node
An NFS share on the SSD media tier, reached from the cluster's virtual network through a private endpoint or service endpoint
An NFS share on the HDD media tier, opened to the cluster's public IP addresses with IP network rules on the storage firewall
An SMB share with Microsoft Entra Kerberos, so that the Linux nodes receive POSIX ownership from their Microsoft Entra accounts
quiz.explain: NFS shares give Linux POSIX semantics, require the SSD media tier and are reached through private or service endpoints. Choice C fails twice: NFS is not offered on HDD, and NFS shares do not accept IP address rules.

quiz.q: A 3 GB contract in the archive tier is needed by the legal team within two hours. No rehydration has been started yet. What should the administrator do?
choices: Download the blob straight from the archive tier with AzCopy, which reads archived data without rehydrating it first
Take a snapshot of the archived blob and read the snapshot, which Azure serves from the hot tier as soon as it is taken
Change the account's default access tier to hot, which brings every archived blob in the account online within an hour
Rehydrate it with Set Blob Tier or Copy Blob to an online tier, choosing High priority, which can finish in under an hour
quiz.explain: High priority rehydration may complete in under an hour for blobs under 10 GB, either in place or as a copy. Choice C is wrong because the default access tier applies only to inferred online tiers and never moves blobs out of archive.

days.recap: Choose SMB for mixed clients and NFS for Linux on SSD behind private networking, size shares through quota or provisioned capacity, set anonymous access per container only, and manage hot, cool, cold and archive tiers with defaults, minimum periods and rehydration priority.

days.title: Blob Data Protection and Lifecycle Management

concepts.heading: Blob Soft Delete
concepts.body: Blob soft delete keeps deleted blobs, snapshots and versions for a retention period of 1 to 365 days, during which you can undelete them. When a blob is overwritten, soft delete also keeps the old data as a soft-deleted snapshot. It does not protect against changes to blob metadata or properties, which need versioning. How you restore depends on versioning. With versioning off, Undelete brings back the soft-deleted blob and its snapshots. With versioning on, deleting a blob turns its current version into a previous version, and Undelete restores soft-deleted versions and snapshots but not the base blob; you restore the blob by promoting a previous version, which the portal calls Make current version. When the retention period ends, the data is deleted permanently, so waiting never restores anything. Microsoft recommends combining blob soft delete with container soft delete and versioning.

concepts.heading: Container Soft Delete
concepts.body: Container soft delete protects whole containers. A deleted container and everything in it, including blobs, versions and snapshots, is kept for 1 to 365 days, with seven days as the default, and can be restored from the portal after selecting Show deleted containers. Several rules trip administrators up. A container can be restored only to its original name, so if someone created a new container with that name, delete or rename it first. Changing the retention period applies only to containers deleted after the change. Container soft delete does not bring back a single blob deleted from a live container; that needs blob soft delete or versioning. Blob soft delete and container soft delete have separate retention periods, so align them. The least privileged built-in role that can restore a container is Storage Blob Data Contributor. A deleted storage account is a different case from a deleted container.

concepts.heading: Blob Versioning and Snapshots
concepts.body: With blob versioning enabled, Azure automatically keeps the previous state of a blob every time it is written or its metadata is set, and each version has its own version ID. No application change is needed, which makes versioning the answer when a faulty job overwrites blobs or edits metadata. To roll back, promote a previous version to be the current version. A blob snapshot is different: it is a manual, point-in-time copy that an application or administrator creates on purpose, for example before a planned update, and Azure never takes snapshots automatically on writes. Versioning is also a prerequisite for object replication on both accounts and, with blob soft delete and change feed, for point-in-time restore of block blobs. Every version is billed for the data it holds, so use a lifecycle rule to delete old versions after a set number of days. Enable versioning with az storage account blob-service-properties update --enable-versioning true.

concepts.heading: Share Snapshots and Share Soft Delete
concepts.body: Azure Files has its own protection features. A share snapshot is a read-only, incremental, point-in-time copy of a whole file share, and a share can keep up to 200. You restore individual files or folders by copying them back from a snapshot, for example through the Previous Versions tab in Windows File Explorer, and Azure Backup can schedule snapshots for you. Soft delete for file shares works only at the share level: it keeps a deleted share and its snapshots for the retention period, 1 to 365 days, and is on by default for new accounts. Snapshots cannot outlive their share, so deleting a share deletes its snapshots, and only undeleting the share, for example with az storage share-rm restore, brings them back. Blob features do not apply to file shares: Undelete Blob, point-in-time restore and lifecycle management all work on blobs, not on Azure Files.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle Management Rules
concepts.body: Lifecycle management moves or deletes blobs automatically through rules in a policy on the account. Each rule has filters, conditions and actions. The blobTypes filter is required, blockBlob or appendBlob. The optional prefixMatch filter must start with the container name, for example app/logs/ for log blobs in container app, and wildcards are not supported. blobIndexMatch filters on blob index tags, and filters combine with AND. Conditions count days after creation, after last modification, or after last access. Actions include tierToCool, tierToCold, tierToArchive and delete, and separate actions can apply to base blobs, previous versions and snapshots. A rule might cool blobs after 30 days without modification, archive them after 180 and delete them after 730. New or changed rules can take up to 24 hours before they first run. A rule that never acts usually has a prefix without the container name.

concepts.heading: Last Access Tracking and Re-Archiving
concepts.body: Two lifecycle details appear often. First, to tier by reads rather than writes, enable access time tracking on the account and use daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan; without tracking, the rule cannot see reads. Adding enableAutoTierToHotFromCool moves a cool blob back to hot when it is accessed again, and it works only with the last access condition. Second, changing a blob's tier does not change its last modified time. A blob modified three years ago that you rehydrate with Set Blob Tier still matches a rule such as tierToArchive after 180 days since modification, so the next policy run archives it again. The fixes are to add daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan to the tierToArchive action, which keeps rehydrated blobs online for a chosen number of days, or to rehydrate by copying to a new blob, which gets a new modified time. Versioning does not help, because rehydration is not a write.

examPoints: A question in which Undelete does not bring back a deleted blob, or a container cannot be restored, is testing how versioning changes blob restore and that containers restore only to their original name.
A question about recovering files deleted from an Azure file share, or snapshots lost with a deleted share, is testing share snapshots for item-level restore and share soft delete for whole shares.

A question in which a lifecycle rule does nothing, or keeps re-archiving rehydrated blobs, is testing prefixes that start with the container name, access time tracking, and daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan.

quiz.q: A lifecycle rule must delete blobs under the raw/ folder of container telemetry 30 days after they were last modified. Which prefixMatch value should the rule use?
choices: raw/, because a prefix is matched against blob names in every container of the account at the same time
raw/*, because a wildcard is required for the prefix to match blobs in nested folders below the raw folder
*/raw/, because the leading wildcard lets the rule match the raw folder in whichever container it appears
telemetry/raw/, because every prefix in a lifecycle rule must start with the name of the container itself
quiz.explain: A lifecycle prefix must begin with the container name, so telemetry/raw/ matches the intended blobs. Choice B fails because lifecycle prefix strings do not support wildcard matching, and raw/* also leaves out the container name.

quiz.q: Container soft delete is set to 7 days. Five days after a container was deleted, an administrator raises the retention to 30 days. When will that deleted container be removed permanently?
choices: Seven days after it was deleted, because a new retention period applies only to containers deleted after the change
Thirty days after it was deleted, because the new retention period applies at once to every soft-deleted container
Thirty-five days after it was deleted, because the new retention period is added to the days that have already passed
Immediately, because changing the retention period purges every container that is in the soft-deleted state at the time
quiz.explain: A changed retention period applies only to containers deleted after the change, so this container keeps its original seven days. Choice B is the natural assumption, which is why it is tested: the new value does not reach containers already deleted.

days.recap: Blob soft delete, container soft delete and versioning protect blobs in different ways, share snapshots and share soft delete protect Azure Files, and lifecycle rules tier or delete blobs using container-prefixed filters, last access tracking and a tier-change condition to avoid re-archiving.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Implement and Manage Storage

concepts.heading: Two Gates: Network and Authorization
concepts.body: Every storage request passes two gates, and many Domain 2 questions hinge on which one failed. The network gate is the storage firewall: virtual network rules with service endpoints for subnets, IP rules for public addresses only, the trusted services exception for services such as Azure Monitor and Azure Backup, resource instance rules for specific resources, and private endpoints. It filters only data plane requests, and same-region traffic never matches IP rules. The authorization gate is either Microsoft Entra ID with data roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader, Shared Key with the account keys, or a SAS. Owner and Contributor do not read data through Entra, and a resource instance rule still needs a data role. When a scenario shows a 403, ask first whether the request came from an allowed network, and only then whether the identity or token has the right permission.

concepts.heading: SAS and Key Revocation Map
concepts.body: Match each credential to its revocation method. A service SAS that references a stored access policy is revoked, shortened or extended by editing, deleting or renaming that policy, with no key change. An ad hoc service SAS or an account SAS is revoked by regenerating the key that signed it, after moving applications to the other key. A user delegation SAS is unaffected by key rotation; revoke it with az storage account revoke-delegation-keys or by removing the creator's role. Setting AllowSharedKeyAccess to false blocks all key-based requests, so only Microsoft Entra requests and user delegation SAS still work. Account SAS is needed for several services in one token or service-level operations, while user delegation SAS is the recommended choice when a token must trace back to an identity. Use sip to limit client addresses and spr=https to refuse plain HTTP.

concepts.heading: Accounts, Redundancy, and Failover Recap
concepts.body: Account type, premium performance and infrastructure encryption are chosen at creation, and changing them means a new account plus an AzCopy copy. Secure transfer rejects HTTP, minimum TLS rejects old TLS, and the account's anonymous access setting overrides containers. LRS and ZRS stay in one region, GRS and GZRS add an unreadable secondary, and RA-GRS and RA-GZRS add a readable -secondary endpoint. Geo and read-access changes are SKU updates, zone changes are conversions, and LRS to GZRS needs both steps. Planned failover suits drills with both regions available and keeps geo-redundancy; unplanned failover can lose recent writes and leaves the account LRS. Object replication needs versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source, and copies only new blobs unless you widen the scope. Customer-managed keys need purge protection and, at creation, a user-assigned identity; encryption scopes separate keys per container.

concepts.heading: Files and Blob Configuration Recap
concepts.body: For Azure Files, SMB serves Windows, Linux and macOS over port 445, while NFS serves Linux only, needs the SSD tier and admits clients only through private or service endpoints. Identity-based SMB access uses one source per account, AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Kerberos, and the more restrictive of the share-level role and NTFS permissions applies. Provisioned v2 bills provisioned storage, IOPS and throughput with a hard size limit, while pay-as-you-go is HDD and SMB only, billed by usage with a quota as a cap. For blobs, anonymous access needs both the account setting and a container level of Blob or Container, set per container only. Hot, cool, cold and archive have minimum periods of none, 30, 90 and 180 days, the default tier moves only inferred blobs, and archived blobs need rehydration, with High priority for urgent ones.

concepts.heading: Data Protection and Lifecycle Recap
concepts.body: Pick the protection feature by what was lost. A deleted blob comes back through blob soft delete, or by promoting a previous version when versioning is on. Overwrites and metadata changes are captured by versioning. A deleted container comes back through container soft delete, only under its original name. Files or folders deleted from an Azure file share come back from share snapshots, and a deleted share, together with its snapshots, comes back through share soft delete. Lifecycle management tiers and deletes blobs by age since creation, modification or last access, with prefixes that start with the container name and no wildcards. Access time tracking enables read-based rules and automatic return to hot, and daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan stops rehydrated blobs from being archived again. Rules can take up to 24 hours to start. Domain 2 is 15 to 20 percent of the exam, so aim for accuracy here.

examPoints: A question that shows a 403 error on a storage request is testing whether you can tell a network rule failure from an authorization failure before choosing a fix.
A question that asks how to cut off or extend access that was handed out is testing the revocation map: stored access policies, key rotation, revoking delegation keys, or disabling Shared Key.
A question about lost data is testing which protection feature matches the loss: blob soft delete, versioning, container soft delete, share snapshots or share soft delete.

quiz.q: A developer's user delegation SAS for a container was sent to the wrong person. The account keys have never been used to sign anything. How can the administrator invalidate the SAS?
choices: Regenerate key1 and key2, because rotating both account keys invalidates every SAS that was issued for the account
Delete the stored access policy on the container, because every user delegation SAS takes its expiry from that policy
Revoke the account's user delegation keys, or remove the role of the principal that requested the delegation key
Set AllowSharedKeyAccess to false, because user delegation SAS requests are authorized through the account keys
quiz.explain: A user delegation SAS is signed with a key obtained through Microsoft Entra ID, so revoking delegation keys or the creator's permissions invalidates it. Choice A is the classic distractor: key rotation revokes only SAS signed with the account keys.

quiz.q: VMs in a subnet in West Europe get 403 errors from a storage account in West Europe. The account allows selected networks, and the administrator has added the VMs' outbound public IP address as an IP rule. What should she do?
choices: Wait an hour for the IP rule to propagate, because new storage firewall rules apply to Azure VMs only after a delay
Add a virtual network rule for the subnet with a storage service endpoint, because IP rules ignore same-region traffic
Enter the address as a /32 range, because the storage firewall matches Azure VMs only when a prefix length is given
Enable the trusted services exception, because VMs in the same subscription count as trusted Azure services for storage
quiz.explain: Requests from the same region reach storage over private Azure addresses, so IP rules never match them and a virtual network rule is required. Choice D is wrong because the trusted services list covers specific Azure services such as Azure Monitor, not your own VMs.

days.recap: Domain 2 comes down to two access gates, a clear revocation map for SAS and keys, account settings fixed at creation, redundancy and failover choices, Files versus Blob configuration, and the right protection feature for each kind of data loss.

days.title: ARM Templates and Bicep: Structure, Parameters, Modes and What-If

concepts.heading: Template Structure: Parameters, Variables, Resources, Outputs
concepts.body: An ARM JSON template has four working sections. Parameters are values supplied at deployment time and can carry a type, a defaultValue and allowedValues; a value outside allowedValues fails validation before anything is deployed. Variables are computed inside the template and cannot be set by the person deploying. Resources describe what to deploy, and outputs return values such as an endpoint when the deployment finishes. Bicep expresses the same ideas more compactly: an @allowed(['Standard_LRS','Standard_GRS']) decorator above param storageSku string = 'Standard_LRS', and sku: { name: storageSku } in the resource. Outputs are stored in the deployment history, so a script can read them later with az deployment group show and a query on properties.outputs. On the exam, a value the deployer must choose belongs in a parameter, a value the template computes belongs in a variable, and a parameter that is declared but never referenced changes nothing.

concepts.heading: Secure Parameters and Parameters Files
concepts.body: Parameter values are recorded with the deployment, so a plain string password can later be read in the deployment history. Marking it with the @secure() decorator in Bicep, or the secureString and secureObject types in ARM JSON, keeps the value out of deployment history, the portal and command-line output while still accepting it at deploy time. Length decorators such as @minLength only validate, and an output is stored in history too, so never return a secret as an output. Values can come from a JSON parameters file or a .bicepparam file that starts with using './main.bicep'. Because that file already names its template, you deploy it with az deployment group create --resource-group rg-prod --parameters prod.bicepparam and no --template-file. A .bicepparam file can also pull a secret from Azure Key Vault with getSecret. Exam signal: a password visible in deployment history means the parameter is missing @secure().

concepts.heading: Dependencies and Loops
concepts.body: Resource Manager deploys independent resources in parallel and orders the rest only by their dependencies; the order in which resources appear in the file is ignored. In Bicep, referencing another resource's symbolic name, such as vnet.properties.subnets[0].id, creates an implicit dependency, and a nested child or a resource with parent: depends on its parent, so an extra dependsOn only slows the deployment. ARM JSON is stricter: a child nested in a parent's resources array does not get an implicit dependency, so you add dependsOn with the parent's resourceId. Loops create several instances: copy with a count in ARM, or a for expression in Bicep. copyIndex() is zero-based, so copyIndex(1) gives 1, 2, 3. Loop instances deploy in parallel unless you set @batchSize(2) in Bicep or mode serial with a batchSize in ARM. Exam signal: a child created before its parent in ARM JSON is fixed with an explicit dependsOn.

concepts.heading: Deployment Modes and What-If
concepts.body: A resource group deployment runs in incremental mode by default: resources in the template are created or updated, and resources already in the group but missing from the template are left alone. Complete mode also deletes those missing resources. Microsoft calls complete mode not recommended and points to deployment stacks when a deployment must delete resources. Incremental does not mean partial at the property level: a redeployed resource gets every property from the template, so a tag added in the portal but absent from the file is removed. Before deploying a change, run az deployment group what-if, or New-AzResourceGroupDeployment with -WhatIf, to see the predicted creates, modifies and deletes without changing anything; --confirm-with-what-if previews and then asks to continue. What-if needs the same permissions as a real deployment. Exam signal: a VM that vanished after a deployment points to complete mode, and a lost portal tag points to properties being reapplied.

concepts.heading: Deployment Scopes
concepts.body: Every deployment targets one scope, and the scope picks the command. A resource group deployment uses az deployment group create --resource-group with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment in PowerShell. A subscription deployment uses az deployment sub create --location, with New-AzSubscriptionDeployment; the management group and tenant equivalents are az deployment mg create and az deployment tenant create. For scopes above the resource group, the location only says where the deployment's own metadata is stored, not where resources go. A Bicep file is resource-group scoped by default; targetScope = 'subscription' lets it declare a Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups resource and then deploy a VNet into that group through a module whose scope is the new group. Complete mode applies to resource group deployments, not to subscription-level ones. Exam signal: a file that creates resource groups fails with az deployment group create because it must be deployed at subscription scope.

concepts.heading: Export and Decompile
concepts.body: There are two ways to get a template from Azure. Exporting from a resource group or resource, for example az group export --name rg-crm > main.json or Export-AzResourceGroup, generates a snapshot of the resources as they are now, including changes made in the portal after the original deployment; the output is autogenerated, with hard-coded values and extra properties, so it needs clean-up. Saving from deployment history returns the exact template that was deployed, ready to redeploy, but without later manual changes. Either JSON file can be converted with az bicep decompile --file main.json, which writes main.bicep beside it. Decompilation is a starting point, not a guaranteed one-to-one translation: Bicep names allow only letters, digits and underscores, so a parameter named Security.Tenant.Id becomes Security_Tenant_Id and old parameter files must be updated. Exam signal: to match a resource group as it is today, export it; to reuse the original deployment exactly, use deployment history.

examPoints: A question in which resources disappear from a resource group, or portal-added tags vanish, after a template deployment is testing the difference between complete mode (deletes resources not in the template) and incremental mode (reapplies all properties of each resource it deploys).
A question that asks how to preview creates, modifies and deletes before touching production is testing what-if (az deployment group what-if or -WhatIf), not az bicep build or a template export.

A question about a password showing up in deployment history, or a .bicepparam deployment failing, is testing the @secure() decorator and the rule that a .bicepparam file is passed with --parameters alone.

quiz.q: A Bicep file starts with targetScope = 'subscription' and creates a resource group plus a module that deploys a storage account into it. Which command deploys it?
choices: az deployment group create --resource-group rg-data --template-file main.bicep, run against an existing group
az deployment mg create --management-group-id mg-prod --template-file main.bicep, run at management group scope
az deployment sub create --location westeurope --template-file main.bicep, run at subscription scope
az deployment group create --mode Complete --template-file main.bicep, so the group is created first
quiz.explain: A file with targetScope = 'subscription' is deployed with az deployment sub create, and the location only stores the deployment metadata. Choice D is tempting, but complete mode only decides whether unlisted resources in a group are deleted; it never changes the scope.

quiz.q: An admin must change a storage account SKU in production but first wants to see exactly which resources and properties the updated template would create, modify or delete, without deploying. What should she run?
choices: az deployment group what-if with the updated template against the production resource group
az bicep build to compile the updated file and compare the JSON with the deployed account
az group export on the production group and compare the result with the updated template by hand
az deployment group create in incremental mode, because incremental mode never changes existing resources
quiz.explain: What-if asks Resource Manager to predict creates, modifies and deletes without changing anything. Choice D is wrong because incremental mode still deploys and reapplies every property of the resources in the template.

days.recap: Templates declare parameters (use @secure() for secrets), dependencies and loops; deploy at the right scope, prefer incremental mode and run what-if first, export a resource group to capture its current state, and decompile JSON to Bicep as a starting point.

days.title: Virtual Machines: Creation, Sizes, Disks, Encryption and Moves

concepts.heading: Creating a VM and Its Security Type
concepts.body: On the Basics tab of the VM create page you choose the subscription, resource group, region, availability options, security type, image, size, administrator account and inbound ports; later tabs cover disks, networking, management, monitoring and extensions. Trusted launch is the default security type for new Generation 2 VMs. It combines Secure Boot, which lets only boot components and kernel drivers signed by trusted publishers load, and vTPM, a virtual TPM 2.0 used for measured boot and attestation; each can be turned on or off separately. That matters for unsigned drivers: Learn notes that the NVIDIA GRID driver on Linux requires Secure Boot to be disabled, which you do in the VM's configuration by clearing Enable Secure Boot rather than rebuilding the VM. Exam signal: a driver or custom kernel that will not load on a new Trusted launch VM points to Secure Boot, not to disk encryption or the VM size.

concepts.heading: Sizes and Resizing
concepts.body: You can resize a VM whether it is running or deallocated, but resizing a running VM always restarts it. A running VM can move only to sizes that the hardware cluster currently hosting it supports, which is why the portal's Size list may not show a size that the region offers for new VMs. Stopping (deallocating) the VM releases the host, and the portal notes that this may reveal more sizes; PowerShell's Get-AzVMSize with -VMName lists sizes for the current cluster. Availability sets add a twist: every VM of a set is allocated on the cluster that hosts the set, so to reach a size that cluster lacks you deallocate all VMs in the set, resize, and start them together. Deallocating releases dynamic IP addresses but leaves OS and data disks untouched. Exam signal: a size missing from the list for a running VM means deallocate first, not delete and re-create.

concepts.heading: OS, Data and Temporary Disks
concepts.body: A VM has an OS disk and optional data disks, both persistent managed disks, plus on most sizes a temporary disk that is local storage on the physical host and not a managed disk. On Windows the temporary disk is drive D: by default; on Linux it is typically /dev/disk/azure/resource. Its data can be lost during maintenance, redeployment or a stop (deallocate), because the VM may return on another host, so it suits page files and tempdb, never logs or data you keep. Growing a disk has two layers: increase the managed disk size in the portal (Size + performance) or with az disk update, then extend the partition in the guest, for example with Disk Management or diskpart extend; shrinking is not supported. Eligible data disks can be expanded while the VM runs, but OS disks need the VM deallocated. Exam signal: files missing from D: after a weekend deallocation means the temporary disk.

concepts.heading: Encryption at Host Versus Azure Disk Encryption
concepts.body: Server-side encryption is always on and encrypts OS and data disks when Azure Storage writes them, with platform-managed keys or customer-managed keys through a disk encryption set; it does not cover the temporary disk or host caches. Encryption at host extends it: the server hosting the VM encrypts the temporary disk, ephemeral OS disks and disk caches, and data flows encrypted to storage, without using the VM's CPU. To use it, register the EncryptionAtHost feature once per subscription, pick a supported size, and deallocate an existing VM before enabling it. It cannot be enabled on a VM that has ever had Azure Disk Encryption, even after decryption. Azure Disk Encryption encrypts volumes inside the guest with BitLocker or DM-Crypt and uses the VM's CPU; it is scheduled for retirement on September 15, 2028, and Microsoft recommends encryption at host for new VMs. Exam signal: a requirement to encrypt temp disks and caches on the host points to encryption at host.

concepts.heading: Moving VMs to Another Resource Group, Subscription or Region
concepts.body: Moving a VM to another resource group or subscription changes only where it is organized. The resource ID changes because it contains the resource group name, the region stays the same, the VM keeps running, and role assignments on the moved resource do not travel and must be re-created. For a subscription move, both subscriptions must be in the same Microsoft Entra tenant, the VM and its dependents such as disks and NICs must sit in one resource group and move together, and a VM in an existing virtual network moves only if the virtual network moves too: consolidate first, then move. A region move is different: Azure Resource Mover adds the VM and its dependencies, prepares replication, initiates the move, then commits it. Public IP addresses are not retained, extensions and role assignments are not copied, and the temporary disk is excluded. Exam signal: a different region needs Resource Mover, not a resource group move.

examPoints: A question in which a needed VM size is missing from the Size list, or a resize fails inside an availability set, is testing that a running VM is limited to its current hardware cluster and that deallocating (all VMs in the set, for a set) frees it.

A question about data lost from drive D: after a deallocation, or a disk grown in Azure that Windows still shows at the old size, is testing the temporary disk and the two-layer disk expansion (Azure size, then extend the volume in the guest).

A question that compares encrypting temp disks and caches with in-guest BitLocker or DM-Crypt is testing encryption at host versus Azure Disk Encryption, including the rule that a VM that ever had ADE cannot enable encryption at host.

quiz.q: An admin moves VM web01 with its NIC and disks from rg-test to rg-prod in the same subscription. A monitoring script that used the VM's resource ID now fails. Why?
choices: The move restarted the VM in a new region, so the script must target the new regional endpoint
The resource ID contains the resource group name, so the ID changed and the script must use the new one
The move created copies of the VM and disks in rg-prod and left the originals behind in rg-test
The VM's role assignments were copied to rg-prod with new IDs, which invalidated the script's token
quiz.explain: A resource group move changes the resource ID because the group name is part of it, while the region stays the same. Choice A is wrong because a move never changes a resource's region and the VM keeps running.

quiz.q: A new Linux VM in a standard D-series size must have its temporary disk and disk caches encrypted on the host, without using the VM's CPU. The VM has never used Azure Disk Encryption. What should the admin enable?
choices: Azure Disk Encryption with DM-Crypt, storing the encryption keys in an Azure Key Vault
Confidential disk encryption, binding the OS disk key to the VM's virtual TPM chip
A disk encryption set with a customer-managed key for server-side encryption only
Encryption at host on the VM, after confirming the EncryptionAtHost feature is registered for the subscription
quiz.explain: Encryption at host encrypts the temporary disk and caches on the host and sends data to storage already encrypted. Choice C is tempting, but server-side encryption with a customer-managed key still does not cover the temporary disk or host caches.

days.recap: Create VMs with the right security type, deallocate to reach sizes the current cluster lacks, keep data off the temporary disk, prefer encryption at host for new VMs, and remember that resource group moves change the ID while region moves need Resource Mover.

days.title: Availability Sets, Availability Zones and Virtual Machine Scale Sets

concepts.heading: Availability Sets: Fault and Update Domains
concepts.body: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains, groups that share a power source and network switch, and update domains, groups restarted together during planned maintenance, with only one update domain restarted at a time. By default VMs are spread over up to three fault domains, and the fault and update domain counts cannot be changed after the set is created. A VM can join an availability set only when it is created: to add an existing VM, delete it while keeping its disks and re-create it in the set from those disks. Learn also warns that deploying a VM, deallocating it and then deploying the next one can leave both on the same fault domain, so keep earlier VMs running while you build the set. Availability sets protect against failures inside one datacenter, not against losing a whole zone. Exam signal: an existing VM that must join a set means delete and re-create, keeping the disks.

concepts.heading: Availability Zones: Zonal and Nonzonal VMs
concepts.body: Availability zones are physically separate groups of datacenters within a region, each with independent power, cooling and networking. A zonal VM is pinned to the zone you choose at creation, such as zone 1. One zonal VM is not resilient by itself; you gain zone resilience by running several VMs in different zones behind a Standard Load Balancer, or a scale set that spans zones. A nonzonal (regional) VM lets Azure place it in any zone, so it might sit in a zone that fails. The VM reliability guide states that moving a zonal VM to a different zone is not supported, nor is converting it to nonzonal; you deploy a new VM in the target zone, for example from snapshots of the existing disks. Exam signal: protecting against a datacenter outage in a region points to zones, while one rack or host failure points to an availability set.

concepts.heading: Scale Set Orchestration Modes
concepts.body: A Virtual Machine Scale Set is created in one of two orchestration modes, and the mode cannot be changed later. Flexible orchestration, the recommended mode, creates standard Azure VMs managed with the normal VM commands, tags and RBAC. It supports Azure Backup for individual instances, mixing Windows and Linux, and mixing Spot and regular-priority instances in one set. Uniform orchestration creates scale set VMs from one identical model that you manage through the scale set VM APIs; Spot must be all or nothing, and Azure Backup is not supported for its instances. Uniform remains in use for platforms such as Service Fabric and AKS node pools. Compared with an availability set, a scale set adds autoscale, instance protection and automatic repairs. Exam signal: a requirement to back up individual instances or mix Spot with regular capacity points to Flexible mode chosen at creation, never a later switch.

concepts.heading: Autoscale Rules and Profiles
concepts.body: Scale sets use Azure Monitor autoscale. A profile sets a minimum, maximum and default instance count plus rules. Host-based metrics such as Percentage CPU, Network In and Disk Read Operations/Sec come from the VMs without installing an agent; each rule compares a metric aggregation, such as the average over ten minutes, with a threshold and then increases or decreases the count by a number, by a percent, or to a target. When a profile has several rules, autoscale scales out if any scale-out rule is met but scales in only when all scale-in rules are met, because removing capacity is the risky direction. Pair every scale-out rule with a scale-in rule and leave a gap between thresholds, such as out above 75 percent and in below 30 percent, to avoid flapping. Schedule-based profiles set different counts for nights or weekends. Exam signal: a set that never scales in usually has one scale-in rule not met.

concepts.heading: Upgrade Policy
concepts.body: The upgrade policy decides how existing instances pick up changes to the scale set model, such as a new image version, size, data disks or extensions. Automatic lets the platform update all instances at the same time in no guaranteed order, which suits dev and test. Rolling updates instances in batches with settings such as batch size and maximum healthy percentage, and needs application health monitoring: the Application Health extension, or for Uniform sets a load balancer health probe; it is the production choice. Manual changes nothing on existing instances: new instances use the latest model, and you upgrade the others when you choose, in the portal under Instances then Upgrade, or with az vmss update-instances and a list of instance IDs. Exam signal: a model updated a day ago while old instances still run the previous image, and only new instances look right, describes the Manual policy waiting for an upgrade.

concepts.heading: Instance Protection and Automatic Repairs
concepts.body: Instance protection is set per instance after it is created. Protect from scale-in keeps autoscale from choosing that instance during scale-in, while upgrades and reimages still apply; set it under Instances, then Protection Policy, or with az vmss update --instance-id 3 --protect-from-scale-in true. Protect from scale set actions also shields the instance from upgrades, reimages and deallocation started by the scale set. A scale-in policy such as NewestVM or OldestVM only sets the removal order for the whole set. Automatic instance repairs replace unhealthy instances; they need the Application Health extension or a load balancer health probe and use a grace period before repairing a new instance. The repair action Replace builds a new instance, Reimage keeps the instance ID, private IP and data disk but gives a fresh OS disk, and Restart keeps everything. Protected instances are not repaired. Exam signal: keep one busy instance from scale-in means protect from scale-in.

examPoints: A question that asks how to add an existing VM to an availability set, or move a zonal VM to another zone, is testing that both are fixed at creation and require deploying a new VM from the existing disks or snapshots.

A question about a scale set that never scales in, or about which instances receive a new image, is testing autoscale rule logic (any rule to scale out, all rules to scale in) and the Automatic, Rolling and Manual upgrade policies.

A question that needs Azure Backup on instances, mixed Spot and regular VMs, or one instance kept during scale-in is testing Flexible orchestration and instance protection rather than scale-in policies or resource locks.

quiz.q: A scale set runs a six-hour export on instance 4. Autoscale must not remove that instance during the export, but it must still receive image upgrades. What should the admin configure?
choices: Protect from scale-in on instance 4, which still allows upgrades and reimages from the scale set
A NewestVM scale-in policy on the scale set so the oldest instances are always kept running
Protect from scale set actions on instance 4, which blocks scale-in as well as all upgrades
A ReadOnly resource lock on the scale set so that no instance can be deleted during the export
quiz.explain: Protect from scale-in keeps autoscale from choosing the instance while upgrades still apply. Choice C is tempting, but protect from scale set actions also blocks the upgrades the admin still needs.

quiz.q: A scale set has rules to scale out when CPU is above 75 percent or memory above 75 percent, and to scale in when CPU is below 30 percent and, in a second rule, when memory is below 50 percent. At night CPU is 15 percent and memory 60 percent, and nothing scales in. Why?
choices: Autoscale scales in only during a schedule-based profile, and this profile has no night schedule
The default instance count overrides the scale-in rules whenever metric data is being collected
Scale-in runs only when every scale-in rule is met, and the memory rule is not met at 60 percent
Host-based memory metrics need the Azure Monitor Agent installed before rules can evaluate them
quiz.explain: Autoscale scales out when any rule is met but scales in only when all scale-in rules agree, and memory at 60 percent fails the below-50 rule. Choice B is wrong because the default count is used only when metrics cannot be read.

days.recap: Availability sets and zones are chosen when a VM is created; scale sets pick Flexible or Uniform once, scale out on any rule and in only on all rules, apply model changes by upgrade policy, and use instance protection and automatic repairs to keep the right instances healthy.

days.title: Containers: Container Registry, Container Instances and Container Apps

concepts.heading: Azure Container Registry Tiers and Geo-Replication
concepts.body: Azure Container Registry has three service tiers: Basic, Standard and Premium. All share the same data plane APIs and Microsoft Entra authentication; they differ in included storage, throughput and features. Premium alone adds geo-replication, private endpoints through Private Link, public IP network rules, customer-managed keys and connected registries. The tier can be changed at any time, for example with az acr update --name contosoacr --sku Premium, with no downtime; moving down from Premium first requires removing Premium-only resources such as replicas. A geo-replicated registry is still one registry with one login server such as contosoacr.azurecr.io, one set of credentials and role assignments, and active-active replicas, so each client pulls from a nearby replica. Replication is eventually consistent, and ACR Tasks run only in the home region. Exam signal: a Standard registry that needs a copy in another region or a private endpoint must move to Premium.

concepts.heading: Registry Authentication and ACR Tasks
concepts.body: The admin user is one shared account per registry with full push and pull rights; it is disabled by default and all its users appear as one user, so policies keep it off. Instead, grant a Microsoft Entra identity a registry role: AcrPull to pull images and AcrPush to push them, assigned at the registry's scope with az role assignment create. Service principals suit headless tools; managed identities avoid stored passwords. Azure Container Instances does not support a system-assigned managed identity for image pulls from a registry, so use a user-assigned identity with AcrPull and name it in the container group's imageRegistryCredentials. ACR Tasks builds images in Azure on a commit, a timer or a base image update; the base-image trigger is enabled by default and tracks the FROM image after the task runs once. Exam signal: a patched base image that triggers no rebuild was pushed under a new tag instead of the stable tag the task follows.

concepts.heading: Container Instances: Groups, Resources and Restart Policy
concepts.body: A container group is the top-level resource in Azure Container Instances: containers on the same host that share a lifecycle, a local network, where they reach each other on localhost, and storage volumes, like a Kubernetes pod. The group is allocated the sum of its containers' CPU and memory requests, and an optional limit lets one container borrow idle capacity up to the group total. The restart policy is Always by default, which keeps restarting a finished task and keeps it running and billed; OnFailure restarts only after a nonzero exit code, and Never does not restart after a successful exit. Some properties, including OS type, CPU and memory resources and the restart policy, cannot be updated in place: delete the group and create it again, for example with az container create --restart-policy OnFailure. Exam signal: a nightly batch container that keeps running after finishing needs OnFailure or Never.

concepts.heading: Container Instances: Secure Values, Volumes and DNS Names
concepts.body: Environment variables configure a container at start. A normal variable is set with value and shows to anyone who can read the container group; a secure value, set with secureValue in YAML or ARM, is available inside the container but only the variable's name appears in the portal and CLI output. A secret volume is another option and mounts secrets as files. Containers are stateless, so data that must survive a restart goes on a mounted volume, most often an Azure file share mounted with --azure-file-volume-share-name and --azure-file-volume-mount-path. Learn lists the limits: Linux containers only, the container runs as root, and you supply the storage account name and key because SMB mounting with managed identity is not supported. A group's public IP can change after a restart or re-creation, so give it a DNS name label such as contoso-api.westeurope.azurecontainer.io. Exam signal: a partner whose hard-coded IP broke needs the DNS name label.

concepts.heading: Container Apps: Revisions and Ingress
concepts.body: In Azure Container Apps a revision is an immutable snapshot of an app version. Changing the template section, such as the image, container settings or scale rules, creates a new revision; changing configuration such as secrets, ingress or the revision mode applies to all revisions. In Single revision mode, the default, a new revision takes all traffic once it is ready and the old one is deprovisioned. Multiple revision mode keeps several revisions active and lets you split traffic by weights that add up to 100, for example with az containerapp ingress traffic set and --revision-weight app-orders--v1=90 app-orders--v2=10; rolling back is setting the weights back. Reachability has two layers: an internal environment, chosen at creation and fixed, has no public endpoint, while app ingress is external (the environment's endpoint) or internal (only apps in the environment). Exam signal: a 90/10 canary needs Multiple revision mode.

concepts.heading: Container Apps: Scale Rules and Resources
concepts.body: Container Apps scales horizontally by adding or removing replicas, driven by KEDA; vertical scaling is not supported, so a rule never changes a replica's CPU or memory. A scale definition sets minimum replicas, which defaults to 0, maximum replicas, which defaults to 10, and rules: HTTP for concurrent requests, TCP for concurrent connections, or custom rules from KEDA scalers such as azure-servicebus or azure-queue, with authentication through a secret or a managed identity. If you add no rule, the default HTTP rule applies; Learn warns that with ingress disabled and neither a minimum of at least 1 nor a custom rule, the app scales to zero and cannot start again. On the Consumption plan, the total CPU and memory of all containers in an app must match one of the allowed pairs, where memory is twice the vCPU, such as 1.5 vCPU with 3.0Gi. Exam signal: a queue worker stuck at zero replicas needs a custom queue scale rule.

examPoints: A question about pulling images from a registry without the admin user, or from Container Instances with a managed identity, is testing AcrPull role assignments and the rule that ACI needs a user-assigned identity for registry pulls.

A question in which a finished ACI task keeps running, a password shows in container properties, or a hard-coded public IP stops working is testing the restart policy, secureValue and the DNS name label.
A question that splits traffic between two versions or keeps a queue worker from stopping at zero replicas is testing Container Apps revision modes and custom KEDA scale rules.

quiz.q: A company's Standard tier container registry in West Europe must also serve image pulls from a local replica in Southeast Asia, using the same login server name. What should the admin do?
choices: Create a second Standard registry in Southeast Asia and import every repository into it on a schedule
Enable the admin user and point hosts in Southeast Asia at the West Europe login server with its password
Move the registry resource to a resource group located in Southeast Asia so pulls are served from there
Change the registry to the Premium tier and add a geo-replica in the Southeast Asia region
quiz.explain: Geo-replication is a Premium feature that keeps one registry and one login server with replicas in several regions, and the tier change has no downtime. Choice A is tempting, but a second registry has a different login server and separate credentials.

quiz.q: An Azure Container Instances group runs a nightly report container that exits with code 0 when done, but the group keeps running and billing all day. It was created with default settings. What should the admin do?
choices: Stop the container group every morning with a scheduled runbook and leave the restart policy unchanged
Delete the group and create it again with the OnFailure restart policy, because the policy cannot be updated
Update the existing group in place with az container create and the Never restart policy value
Add a liveness probe that fails after the report finishes so the platform removes the container
quiz.explain: The default restart policy is Always, and the restart policy is one of the properties that requires deleting and re-creating the group. Choice C is wrong because the restart policy cannot be changed by updating the existing group.

days.recap: Container Registry tiers decide features such as geo-replication, ACI groups need the right restart policy, secure values and volumes, and Container Apps uses revisions for traffic splitting and KEDA rules for horizontal scaling.

days.title: App Service Plans, Scaling and Deployment Slots

concepts.heading: App Service Plan Tiers and Features
concepts.body: An App Service plan defines the VMs that run your apps, and its pricing tier decides both the VM size and the features. Free and Shared run apps on shared VMs with CPU quotas and cannot scale out. Basic gives dedicated VMs with manual scale out, custom domains, certificates, backups, VNet integration and private endpoints. Standard adds deployment slots and autoscale. Premium v2, v3 and v4 add larger VMs, more instances and slots, and the HTTP-based automatic scaling option. IsolatedV2 runs in an App Service Environment inside your own virtual network. Every app in a plan shares its tier, region and OS. Changing the tier takes seconds and needs no redeployment, for example az appservice plan update --name plan-intranet --resource-group rg-web --sku S1. Exam signal: a Basic plan that needs a staging slot or rule-based autoscale must scale up to Standard or higher.

concepts.heading: Scale Up Versus Scale Out
concepts.body: Scaling up changes the plan's tier or size, for example S1 to P1v3, so every instance gets more CPU, memory and disk, and higher tiers unlock features. Scaling out changes the number of instances that run the apps, so more instances share the requests. The difference matters when you read a symptom. If many requests overload the app, scaling out spreads them across instances. If a single request needs more memory than one instance has, more instances change nothing, because that request still runs on one instance with the same memory; the fix is scaling up. Both actions affect every app in the plan, because apps run on the plan's instances, and you pay for the plan's instances whether one app or ten use them. Exam signal: out-of-memory errors on one large request mean scale up, and high CPU from many users means scale out.

concepts.heading: Autoscale and Per-App Scaling
concepts.body: From Standard upward, Scale out (App Service plan) can use custom autoscale through Azure Monitor: profiles with a minimum, maximum and default instance count, metric rules such as CPU percentage or memory percentage, and schedule profiles for known busy times. As with scale sets, autoscale scales out if any scale-out rule is met but scales in only when every scale-in rule is met, so keep a margin between thresholds. Premium tiers also offer automatic scaling, where the platform scales on HTTP traffic. By default every app in a plan runs on all of the plan's instances, so a small admin app scales with a busy storefront. Per-app scaling fixes that: set perSiteScaling to true on the plan and numberOfWorkers on the app to cap how many instances it uses; billing still follows the plan's instance count. Exam signal: one app that must stay on two instances while the plan scales to ten points to per-app scaling.

concepts.heading: Moving Apps Between Plans
concepts.body: An app takes its region and operating system from its plan, so moving an app to another plan has rules. The source and target plans must be in the same resource group and the same region, they must have the same OS type, and they must be in the same deployment unit, which plans created in the same resource group, region and OS share. The Change App Service plan pane therefore lists only plans that qualify, and VNet integration must be disconnected before the move. Moving a Windows app to a Linux plan is not supported: create a new app in the Linux plan and deploy the code. A plan's region cannot be changed either, so moving an app to another region means cloning or redeploying it. Exam signal: when the target plan is in another resource group or runs another OS, the answer is a new app in that plan plus a redeployment, not a plan change.

concepts.heading: Deployment Slots and Swap Settings
concepts.body: Deployment slots, available from Standard upward, are live apps with their own hostnames, such as app-shop-staging. You deploy to staging, test it, then swap it with production so the new version goes live with no downtime, and swapping back rolls it back. A swap exchanges content and most configuration. App settings and connection strings follow the content unless you mark them as Deployment slot setting, or use --slot-settings in the CLI, which keeps the value tied to the slot so production always keeps the production database. Some settings always stay with the slot, including custom domains, non-public certificates and TLS settings, scale settings, managed identities and VNet integration. Exam signal: after a swap, production points to the test database because the connection string was not marked as a slot setting.

concepts.heading: Swap Warm-Up and Swap Behavior
concepts.body: Before a swap switches routing, App Service applies the target slot's slot-specific settings to the source slot's instances, restarts them and warms them up. By default it sends a request to the root path on each instance, and any HTTP response counts as warm, which is too early for an app that answers before its caches load. Two app settings tune this: WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH, such as /health, and WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_STATUSES, such as 200. If an instance returns a code that is not in the list, the swap stops and production keeps running the old version. On Windows, applicationInitialization in Web.config can also list warm-up pages. Because the swap only changes routing once every instance is warm, users see no cold start. Exam signal: users hitting a slow or failing app right after a swap need a custom warm-up path and status codes.

examPoints: A question about a plan that lacks slots or autoscale, or an app that runs out of memory on single requests, is testing tier features and scale up (bigger instances) versus scale out (more instances).
A question where production uses the staging database after a swap, or users hit an unready app right after a swap, is testing Deployment slot settings and the swap warm-up app settings.

A question about one small app scaling with a busy app in the same plan, or moving an app to a Linux plan or another region, is testing per-app scaling and the same-resource-group, region and OS rule for plan changes.

quiz.q: A reporting app in a Standard S1 plan fails with out-of-memory errors whenever one large report is generated. The plan already runs three instances at low CPU. What should the admin do?
choices: Scale out the plan to six instances so that each report request gets more memory available
Enable per-app scaling and set numberOfWorkers on the app so it uses every plan instance
Scale up the plan to a Premium v3 size that gives each instance more memory for each request
Add a staging slot and swap it into production so the report runs on fresh instances
quiz.explain: One request runs on one instance, so only a larger instance size gives it more memory. Choice A is tempting, but more instances only share more requests; each instance still has the same memory.

quiz.q: After swapping staging into production, the production app starts using the test database stored in the staging slot's connection string. What should the admin have configured?
choices: Mark the connection string in each slot as a Deployment slot setting so it stays with its slot
Store the connection string in the production slot only, leaving the staging slot without a value
Set WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH so the swap waits until the database connection is verified
Enable per-app scaling on the plan so each slot keeps its own configuration and instances
quiz.explain: Connection strings follow the content in a swap unless they are marked as slot settings, which keeps each value tied to its slot. Choice C only changes how instances are warmed up and never decides which settings move.

days.recap: The plan tier decides features, scale up for bigger instances and out for more of them, cap small apps with per-app scaling, and use slots with slot settings and custom warm-up for zero-downtime releases.

days.title: App Service Domains, Certificates, Backups and Networking

concepts.heading: Custom Domains
concepts.body: Mapping a custom domain to an App Service app needs a paid tier and two DNS records at the domain provider. The mapping record sends traffic to the app: a subdomain such as www.fabrikam.com uses a CNAME to app-name.azurewebsites.net, while the root domain fabrikam.com uses an A record to the app's IP address, because DNS does not allow a CNAME at the zone apex. The verification record is a TXT record named asuid for the root, or asuid.www for the subdomain, that holds the app's domain verification ID; it proves ownership and protects against subdomain takeover. Prefer CNAMEs for subdomains, because the app's IP address can change. The domain must be in a public DNS zone, which can be Azure DNS or another provider. Exam signal: a root domain that fails validation usually lacks the A record or the asuid TXT record, and a CNAME at the root is never the fix.

concepts.heading: Certificates and TLS Bindings
concepts.body: A custom domain needs a private certificate, one that includes its private key, bound with an SNI SSL or IP-based SSL binding. The free App Service managed certificate needs Basic or higher and is renewed automatically, but it cannot be a wildcard or exported, and for a root domain the app must be reachable from the internet with no IP restrictions, because issuance and renewal depend on that. An App Service certificate is bought and managed in Azure. You can also import a certificate from Key Vault, where App Service needs read access such as the Key Vault Certificate User role, or upload a password-protected PFX file with its full chain. On the TLS side, set the minimum inbound TLS version, 1.2 by default for new apps, and turn on HTTPS Only to redirect HTTP. Exam signal: a wildcard certificate means upload a PFX or import from Key Vault.

concepts.heading: Backups: Automatic and Custom
concepts.body: App Service backups need Basic or higher. Automatic backups run hourly with a fixed 30-day retention, need no configuration and cannot be downloaded. Custom backups write a ZIP file and XML manifest to a container in your own storage account, on demand or on a schedule, with retention from 0 to 30 days or indefinite, so you can download or archive them; there is no 90-day option, so long retention means indefinite plus a cleanup rule. Custom backups reach storage with a SAS URL; managed identity is not supported. If the storage firewall allows only selected networks, use VNet integration, allow the integrated subnet on the storage account and select Backup/restore over virtual network integration. Exam signal: a requirement to download backups or keep them longer than 30 days points to custom backups, and failures after a storage firewall change point to the virtual network backup option.

concepts.heading: VNet Integration for Outbound Traffic
concepts.body: App Service networking features each work in one direction. Virtual network integration handles outbound traffic: it lets the app call resources in or through a virtual network, such as an API on a VM at 10.20.1.4 that has no public IP address. It is available from Basic upward and needs a dedicated subnet in the same region, delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms, with one address per plan instance, so size the subnet with room for scale; Learn notes that a /26 covers a multitenant plan's maximum. Private traffic goes into the virtual network, and with outbound internet traffic routing enabled all outbound traffic does, so NSGs and route tables apply. VNet integration gives no inbound access: the app stays public unless you add a private endpoint or access restrictions. Example: az webapp vnet-integration add --name app-orders --resource-group rg-web --vnet vnet-prod --subnet snet-appsvc-int. Exam signal: an app that must call a private VM needs VNet integration, not a private endpoint.

concepts.heading: Private Endpoints and DNS
concepts.body: A private endpoint handles inbound traffic: it gives the app a private IP address in your virtual network through Private Link, and you can then disable public network access. Name resolution is the part that breaks. With an endpoint in place, app-hr.azurewebsites.net becomes a CNAME to app-hr.privatelink.azurewebsites.net. If clients can resolve that private name to the endpoint's IP, traffic stays private; if not, the name resolves to the public IP, and with public access disabled the request returns 403. The fix is an Azure DNS private zone named privatelink.azurewebsites.net, linked to the virtual network, with A records for the app and its scm site, which a private DNS zone group on the endpoint can create automatically. On-premises clients need DNS forwarding to Azure or their own records. Exam signal: VMs that get 403 after a private endpoint was added need the private DNS zone linked to their network.

concepts.heading: Access Restrictions
concepts.body: Access restrictions are a priority-ordered list of allow and deny rules evaluated on the App Service front ends. Once one rule exists, unmatched requests are denied by default and receive HTTP 403. Rules can match IPv4 or IPv6 ranges, service tags such as AzureFrontDoor.Backend, or virtual network subnets through Microsoft.Web service endpoints, and the scm deployment site can have its own rules. Any rule can add HTTP header filters. That is how you lock an app to your own Azure Front Door profile: the AzureFrontDoor.Backend ranges are shared by every Front Door customer, so the allow rule combines the service tag with an X-Azure-FDID header filter that holds your profile's ID, for example with Add-AzWebAppAccessRestrictionRule and -ServiceTag AzureFrontDoor.Backend plus -HttpHeader. Exam signal: an app that must accept traffic only from one Front Door profile needs the service tag plus the X-Azure-FDID header.

examPoints: A question about mapping fabrikam.com versus www.fabrikam.com, or about a free managed certificate that will not issue, is testing the A record plus asuid TXT for a root domain, CNAME for subdomains, and the managed certificate limits (no wildcard, no IP restrictions).

A question in which an app must call a private VM, or clients must reach the app privately and get 403, is testing VNet integration (outbound) versus private endpoints (inbound) and the privatelink.azurewebsites.net private DNS zone.
A question about downloadable backups, retention beyond 30 days, or allowing only one Front Door profile is testing custom backups and access restrictions with service tags and header filters.

quiz.q: A web app in a Premium v3 plan must call an internal API on a VM at 10.20.1.4 in vnet-prod, which has no public IP. The app itself must stay reachable from the internet. What should the admin configure?
choices: A private endpoint for the app in vnet-prod, with public network access disabled on the app
Virtual network integration with a dedicated subnet in vnet-prod delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms
An access restriction rule that allows the vnet-prod subnet through a Microsoft.Web service endpoint
A custom domain with an A record for the VM's private IP address in a public DNS zone
quiz.explain: VNet integration handles the app's outbound calls into the virtual network and leaves inbound access public. Choice A is tempting, but a private endpoint only handles inbound traffic to the app and disabling public access breaks the internet requirement.

quiz.q: A compliance rule requires monthly backups of a Standard-tier web app that the team can download and keep for 90 days. Only automatic backups exist today. What should the admin configure?
choices: Raise the automatic backup retention to 90 days in the Backups blade of the app
Create a private endpoint so the automatic backups can be copied to an on-premises server
Swap a staging slot into production each month so the old version is kept as a backup
Custom backups to a storage account on a monthly schedule with retention set to indefinite
quiz.explain: Custom backups land in your storage account where they can be downloaded, and since retention offers 0 to 30 days or indefinite, 90 days needs indefinite plus cleanup. Choice A is wrong because automatic backup retention is fixed at 30 days and those backups cannot be downloaded.

days.recap: Map custom domains with the right records, pick a certificate source that fits wildcards and restrictions, use custom backups for downloadable or long-kept copies, and keep VNet integration (outbound), private endpoints with private DNS (inbound) and access restrictions (filtering) apart.

days.title: Domain 3 Review: Deploy and Manage Azure Compute Resources

concepts.heading: Templates: Modes, Scopes and Safety
concepts.body: Domain 3 started with infrastructure as code. Keep four ideas straight. Incremental mode, the default, keeps resources that are not in the template but reapplies every property of the ones that are, so portal-only changes such as tags can disappear; complete mode deletes resources missing from the template and is not recommended. What-if, through az deployment group what-if or -WhatIf, previews creates, modifies and deletes before anything changes. The command must match the file's scope: group, sub, mg or tenant, with a location for the higher scopes. Secrets go in @secure() parameters, never outputs, and a .bicepparam file is passed with --parameters alone. When you need the current state of a resource group, export it; when you need the original deployment, take it from deployment history; and decompile JSON to Bicep as a starting point. Most template questions turn on one of these four.

concepts.heading: Virtual Machines: Size, Disks, Encryption and Moves
concepts.body: For VMs, read the symptom. A size missing from the list for a running VM means deallocate it, and in an availability set deallocate every VM. Files lost from drive D: after a deallocation mean the temporary disk, and a disk that Windows still shows at the old size needs the volume extended in the guest after the Azure resize. Encrypting temp disks and caches on the host means encryption at host, which requires the subscription feature, a deallocated VM and no Azure Disk Encryption history. A resource group or subscription move changes the resource ID, keeps the region, drops role assignments and needs dependents, including the virtual network for a subscription move, in one group. A region move uses Azure Resource Mover, gives the VM a new public IP and does not copy extensions. Those six patterns cover most VM troubleshooting items.

concepts.heading: Availability and Scale Sets: What Is Fixed at Creation
concepts.body: Several compute choices cannot be changed later, and the exam rewards knowing which. A VM joins an availability set only when it is created, the set's fault and update domain counts are fixed, a zonal VM cannot move to another zone, and a scale set's orchestration mode, Flexible or Uniform, is chosen once. The fix in each case is to deploy something new, usually from the existing disks or snapshots. What you can change freely is behavior: autoscale profiles and rules, where any rule scales out and only all rules together scale in; the upgrade policy, Automatic, Rolling or Manual; instance protection on single instances; and automatic repairs with Replace, Reimage or Restart. When a question asks how to change something fixed in place, look for the answer that re-creates it; when it asks about runtime behavior, look for the matching setting.

concepts.heading: Containers: Pick the Service, Then the Setting
concepts.body: Container questions start with the service. Azure Container Registry stores images: Premium is the tier for geo-replication and private endpoints, AcrPull and AcrPush are the roles for Entra identities, and ACR Tasks rebuild on a base image update when it keeps the same tag. Azure Container Instances runs a container group on demand: the restart policy, Always by default, decides whether a finished task keeps running, secureValue hides a secret, an Azure file share keeps data for Linux containers, a DNS name label survives IP changes, and a user-assigned identity pulls from a registry. Azure Container Apps runs scalable apps: Multiple revision mode splits traffic, ingress and the environment's accessibility decide who reaches the app, and KEDA scale rules add replicas, with a custom rule needed for queue workers when ingress is off.

concepts.heading: App Service: Plan, Slots and Network Direction
concepts.body: App Service questions usually hinge on the plan tier, the slot settings or the direction of traffic. The tier decides features: slots and autoscale start at Standard, and a single heavy request needs scaling up, not out. Per-app scaling caps a small app's share of the plan, and an app can move only to a plan in the same resource group, region and OS. In a swap, settings marked as Deployment slot setting stay put, and custom warm-up settings keep users from hitting an unready app. For security, a root domain uses an A record plus asuid TXT, the free managed certificate has no wildcard and needs public reachability, and custom backups give downloadable copies. For networking, VNet integration carries outbound calls, a private endpoint with the privatelink.azurewebsites.net zone handles inbound private access, and access restrictions filter callers.

examPoints: A question that asks how to change something fixed at creation, such as availability set membership, a VM's zone, a scale set's orchestration mode or an ACI restart policy, is testing that the answer is to re-create the resource rather than edit a setting.

A question that mixes App Service networking features is testing direction: VNet integration for outbound calls, a private endpoint plus private DNS for inbound private access, and access restrictions to filter who may call the app.
Domain 3 carries 20-25 percent of the exam, so practise reading each compute symptom (missing size, lost D: data, swap surprises, stuck scale-in) back to the single setting that causes it.

quiz.q: Which change can an administrator make in place, without deploying a new resource?
choices: Switching a scale set's upgrade policy from Manual to Rolling once application health monitoring is set up
Moving a running zonal VM from availability zone 1 into availability zone 2 of the same region
Adding an existing VM that was created without a set to an availability set with other VMs
Changing a scale set's orchestration mode from Uniform to Flexible to enable Azure Backup
quiz.explain: The upgrade policy is a scale set setting that can be changed, while the other three are fixed when the resource is created. Choice D is tempting because Flexible mode does support Azure Backup, but the orchestration mode cannot be changed after creation.

quiz.q: A container app processes messages from a Service Bus queue. Ingress is disabled, minimum replicas is 0, and no scale rule was added. Messages pile up and no replica runs. What should the admin add?
choices: An HTTP scale rule with a lower concurrent request threshold so replicas start sooner
A second revision in Multiple revision mode with 50 percent of the traffic assigned to it
A custom azure-servicebus scale rule that watches the queue length and starts replicas
More CPU and memory for the container so a single replica can drain the queue faster
quiz.explain: With ingress disabled and no custom rule, the app scales to zero and nothing can start it, so a KEDA azure-servicebus rule is needed. Choice A fails because an HTTP rule reacts to requests that never arrive when ingress is off.

days.recap: Domain 3 in one pass: deploy templates safely (incremental, what-if, right scope, @secure()), troubleshoot VMs by symptom, know what is fixed at creation, pick the right container service and setting, and keep App Service tiers, slot settings and traffic direction apart.

days.title: Virtual Networks, Subnets, and Peering

concepts.heading: Address Spaces and Subnets
concepts.body: A virtual network is a private network in one region and one subscription. You give it one or more address spaces, usually private ranges such as 10.20.0.0/16, and divide them into subnets such as snet-web 10.20.1.0/24 and snet-data 10.20.2.0/24. Every network interface takes its private IP from the subnet it sits in, and network security groups and route tables are attached per subnet. Plan the ranges before you build: address spaces must not overlap with on-premises networks or with any virtual network you will peer or connect later, because overlapping ranges cannot be routed. You can add a further address range to an existing virtual network when it runs short. When a question describes a new network for a workload that will later connect to the office or to other networks, the deciding detail is a non-overlapping, generously sized address plan.

concepts.heading: Five Addresses Azure Reserves
concepts.body: Azure keeps five addresses in every subnet, whatever its size: the network address, the first address after it for the default gateway, the next two to map Azure DNS into the virtual network, and the last address as broadcast. In 10.20.4.0/27 the VMs can use 10.20.4.4 to 10.20.4.30, which is 27 addresses. The quick rule is 2 to the power (32 minus prefix) minus 5: a /29, the smallest supported IPv4 subnet, leaves 3, a /28 leaves 11, a /27 leaves 27 and a /26 leaves 59. So 14 single-NIC VMs need a /27, because a /28 falls three addresses short. Exam items love the on-premises habit of subtracting only two addresses; in Azure you always subtract five, even in a small subnet.

concepts.heading: Subnet Delegation and Special Subnets
concepts.body: Some services place their own instances inside your network, and subnet delegation hands a subnet to one such service by name, for example Microsoft.Web/serverFarms for App Service virtual network integration or Microsoft.Sql/managedInstances for SQL Managed Instance. App Service integration needs an unused subnet of at least /28, and Learn recommends /26 to cover a plan at full scale, because each instance takes an address and the size cannot change after assignment. A delegated subnet belongs to that service, so keep private endpoints in a separate subnet. Other subnets have fixed names: GatewaySubnet holds only the virtual network gateway, and AzureBastionSubnet holds only Azure Bastion. If a deployment fails because the chosen subnet already contains VMs or is the gateway subnet, the fix is a new, empty, correctly delegated subnet.

concepts.heading: Peering Is Two Links
concepts.body: Virtual network peering connects two virtual networks so their resources talk over private IPs on the Microsoft backbone, in the same region or across regions, subscriptions and even Microsoft Entra tenants. A peering is not one shared object: each network holds its own link to the other. With only one link created, the state shows Initiated and no traffic flows; only Connected on both sides carries traffic, and if one link is later deleted the other shows Disconnected and you recreate both. With the CLI, az network vnet peering create makes one link in the network named by --vnet-name, so a script needs two commands.
