Peering requires non-overlapping address spaces and is not transitive: two spokes peered to one hub cannot reach each other unless you peer them directly or route through an appliance in the hub.

concepts.heading: Gateway Transit
concepts.body: In a hub-and-spoke design you can share one VPN or ExpressRoute gateway in the hub with every peered spoke instead of building a gateway per network. Two settings are needed, one on each side. Allow gateway transit goes on the peering link in the network that owns the gateway, the hub. Use remote gateways goes on the peering link in the spoke, which has no gateway of its own. The spoke then learns the on-premises routes with the next hop type virtual network gateway. A virtual network can use only one gateway, local or remote, so a network with its own gateway cannot use remote gateways, and Use remote gateways can be enabled on only one of its peerings. When a spoke cannot reach on-premises through the hub, check which of these two switches is missing and on which side.

concepts.heading: Resizing a Peered Network and Sync
concepts.body: You can change the address space of a virtual network that is already peered without tearing the peering down: modify an existing range, add a range or remove an unused one. The peer, however, keeps its own copy of the remote address space. After each change you must sync the peering from every remote network, in the portal by opening Peerings, selecting the link and choosing Sync. Until then the peer has no route for the new range, so VMs in a newly added subnet are unreachable from the peer while older subnets work fine, and the peer's effective routes show no virtual network peering route for the new prefix. Learn recommends syncing after every resize instead of batching changes. If a question says the new subnet is the only thing that cannot be reached across a peering, the answer is sync.

examPoints: A question that gives a VM count and asks for the smallest subnet is testing the five reserved addresses: usable addresses are 2^(32 - prefix) minus 5.
A question where one peering shows Initiated, or where two spokes of one hub cannot talk, is testing that peering needs a link on each side and is not transitive.
A question about a spoke using the hub's VPN gateway is testing Allow gateway transit on the hub link and Use remote gateways on the spoke link.

quiz.q: An administrator peers vnet-hub with vnet-app and vnet-db. VMs in vnet-app cannot reach VMs in vnet-db, although both peerings show Connected. What is the simplest supported fix?
choices: Enable Allow forwarded traffic on both hub peerings, which makes the hub pass traffic between the spokes automatically
Create a direct peering between vnet-app and vnet-db, because peering is not transitive through the hub network
Enable Use remote gateways on both spoke peerings so the spokes share the hub's routing and reach each other
Sync both peerings from the hub, because the spokes have not yet learned each other's address spaces
quiz.explain: Peering is not transitive, so spokes of one hub need a direct peering, or an appliance in the hub with user-defined routes. Choice A is tempting because Allow forwarded traffic is a real peering setting, but it only accepts traffic forwarded by an appliance; it does not create routes between the spokes by itself.

quiz.q: A team adds the range 10.31.0.0/16 to vnet-shared, which is peered with vnet-prod. VMs in the new range cannot be reached from vnet-prod, but older subnets work. What should the administrator do?
choices: Delete both peering links and create them again so that the new address range is included in the peering
Enable Allow gateway transit on the vnet-shared link so the new range is advertised to the peer network
Add a user-defined route in vnet-prod for 10.31.0.0/16 with the next hop type set to virtual network
Sync the peering so that vnet-prod learns the updated address space of vnet-shared
quiz.explain: After a peered network's address space changes, syncing the peering updates the peer's copy and adds the missing route. Choice A would also work in the end, but deleting the links interrupts traffic for the working subnets, and Learn supports resizing in place followed by sync.

days.recap: Size subnets with the five reserved addresses in mind, keep address spaces non-overlapping, and remember that peering is two links, is not transitive, needs gateway transit settings on both sides to share a gateway, and must be synced after a resize.

days.title: Public IPs, Routing, and Connectivity Troubleshooting

concepts.heading: Standard Public IP Addresses
concepts.body: New public IP addresses use the Standard SKU; Basic public IPs were retired on 30 September 2025 and existing ones must be upgraded. A Standard public IP is always static: the address is assigned when the resource is created and kept until you delete the resource, which is what allowlists and DNS A records need. Standard IPs are secure by default, so inbound traffic is blocked until a network security group allows it, and they support availability zones as zonal or zone-redundant. A public IP's zone setting is fixed at creation, so to survive a zone outage you create a new zone-redundant IP and move the frontend to it. For example, az network public-ip create --sku Standard --allocation-method Static creates the address, and the NSG must then allow the inbound port. A question where a new Standard IP answers nothing usually points to a missing NSG rule.

concepts.heading: Public IP Prefixes
concepts.body: A public IP prefix reserves a contiguous range of public addresses in one region and subscription. You then create individual Standard static public IPs from the prefix and attach them to VM network interfaces, Standard load balancers or NAT gateways. Because the range is contiguous, a partner can allow all of your addresses with one firewall rule, even as you add VMs later. You choose only the size, for example /28 for 16 addresses or /29 for 8, and Azure picks the range; the size cannot be changed after creation, and the whole prefix counts against the regional public IP quota from the moment it exists. So size it for growth: if six VMs today may become twelve, a /28 avoids asking the partner for a second rule. When a scenario stresses a predictable, allowlistable block of outbound or inbound addresses, think public IP prefix.

concepts.heading: System Routes and User-Defined Routes
concepts.body: Every subnet gets system routes: one for the virtual network's own address space, routes added by peering and gateways, a default route to the Internet, and routes that drop traffic to unused private ranges with next hop None. A route table holds user-defined routes and is associated with subnets, at most one table per subnet. For each packet Azure picks the route with the longest prefix match; only when prefixes are equal does the source decide, user-defined first, then BGP, then system. That is why a 10.0.0.0/8 route to a firewall loses to a 10.1.0.0/16 peering route; the fix is a user-defined route with the exact peer prefix. Do not put a 0.0.0.0/0 route or an NSG on GatewaySubnet. When traffic ignores your route table, compare prefix lengths before anything else.

concepts.heading: Network Virtual Appliances and IP Forwarding
concepts.body: To force traffic through a firewall VM, you add a user-defined route such as 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop type Virtual appliance and the appliance's private IP, for example 10.0.2.4. The appliance must forward packets that are not addressed to it, which needs two switches. In Azure, enable IP forwarding on the appliance's network interface; it is off by default, and without it Azure drops packets whose destination is not the NIC's own address. Inside the VM, the operating system or firewall software must also forward traffic. The CLI command az network nic update --ip-forwarding true sets the Azure side. Place the appliance in its own subnet, not in a subnet whose route table points at it. If effective routes look perfect but packets die at the appliance, the missing piece is usually IP forwarding on the NIC.

concepts.heading: Effective Routes and Next Hop
concepts.body: Two tools show where a VM's traffic actually goes. Effective routes, on the VM's network interface, list every route that applies to that NIC, system and user-defined, with the source and the next hop; they are shown only while the VM is running. Network Watcher next hop takes a VM, a source IP and a destination IP and returns one answer: the next hop type, such as Internet, VirtualAppliance, VirtualNetworkPeering or None, the next hop IP and the route table that matched, or System Route. A result of None with System Route for a 10.50.1.4 destination means only a default drop route matched, so the peering or address range you expected does not exist or is not Connected. When a question asks why a packet goes the wrong way, choose next hop or effective routes, not NSG tools.

concepts.heading: IP Flow Verify
concepts.body: IP flow verify in Network Watcher answers a different question: will a network security group allow this packet? You give it one VM's network interface, a direction, TCP or UDP, a local IP and port and a remote IP and port. It evaluates every NSG on that NIC and its subnet, plus Azure Virtual Network Manager admin rules, and returns Access allowed or Access denied with the name of the deciding rule. It checks one side at a time: a test on the web VM covers only its outbound rules, so if that says allowed, run the inbound test on the database VM to find the blocking rule. A Network Watcher instance must exist in the VM's region; it is enabled automatically when you create a virtual network. If both sides are allowed, look at routes with next hop, or at the guest firewall.

examPoints: A question where a route to a firewall is ignored is testing longest prefix match first, then the user-defined over BGP over system tiebreak for equal prefixes.
A question where traffic reaches a firewall VM but goes no further is testing IP forwarding on the appliance's Azure network interface.
A question that asks which Network Watcher tool names the NSG rule that blocks a flow is testing IP flow verify, while one about the path a packet takes is testing next hop.

quiz.q: A route table on snet-app sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a firewall VM at 10.0.2.4. Effective routes on the app VMs show the route, but outbound traffic never leaves the firewall. The firewall software is configured to forward. What is most likely missing?
choices: IP forwarding enabled on the firewall VM's Azure network interface, which is off by default
A Standard public IP prefix assigned to the app subnet so that outbound traffic has a source address
An NSG rule on snet-app that allows outbound traffic to the VirtualNetwork service tag and port 443
Route propagation disabled on the firewall subnet so that BGP routes stop overriding the default route
quiz.explain: Without IP forwarding on its Azure NIC, Azure drops packets the appliance tries to forward because their destination is not the NIC's address. Choice C is tempting because NSGs often cause outages, but the default outbound rules already allow this traffic, and the packets do reach the firewall.

quiz.q: A VM cannot reach a SQL VM in another subnet on TCP 1433. IP flow verify run on the web VM for outbound traffic returns Access allowed. What should the administrator do next?
choices: Run Network Watcher next hop on the SQL VM, because next hop also evaluates the inbound NSG rules on that NIC
Conclude that NSGs are not the cause and restart both VMs so that their network interfaces reload the rules
Run IP flow verify on the SQL VM for the inbound direction, because each test evaluates only one VM's NSGs
Open the activity log for the subnet, because denied packets are recorded there with the matching rule name
quiz.explain: IP flow verify checks one network interface at a time, so the inbound rules on the SQL VM's NIC and subnet still need testing. Choice A is tempting because next hop is a real Network Watcher tool, but it reports routing only and never evaluates NSG rules.

days.recap: Standard public IPs are static and closed until an NSG allows traffic, prefixes give a fixed allowlistable block, routes are chosen by longest prefix, appliances need IP forwarding, and next hop, effective routes and IP flow verify each answer a different troubleshooting question.

days.title: Network Security Groups, Application Security Groups, and Azure Bastion

concepts.heading: How NSG Rules Are Evaluated
concepts.body: A network security group holds inbound and outbound rules, each with a priority between 100 and 4096, a source, a destination, a port, a protocol and an action. Rules are processed from the lowest number up, and processing stops at the first match, so an allow rule only works if its number is lower than any broader deny rule. NSGs are stateful: when a flow is allowed, the return traffic is allowed automatically. Every NSG also ends with default rules that you cannot delete: AllowVnetInBound at 65000, AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound at 65001 and DenyAllInBound at 65500, with matching outbound rules that allow virtual network and internet traffic. For example, a deny rule at 200 blocks an allow rule at 300 for the same port. When a rule you created seems to have no effect, compare priorities first.

concepts.heading: Subnet and NIC NSGs Together
concepts.body: You can associate an NSG with a subnet, with a network interface, or with both. Inbound traffic is evaluated by the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG; outbound traffic by the NIC NSG first and then the subnet NSG. Every NSG on the path must allow the flow, so an allow in one and a deny in the other still blocks it. Learn advises associating an NSG with either the subnet or the NIC, not both, because overlapping rules are hard to troubleshoot. The default AllowVnetInBound rule lets every subnet reach every other subnet, so blocking east-west traffic needs an explicit deny numbered below 65000. Effective security rules on a NIC combine both NSGs into one view, but only while the VM is running. When a question shows two NSGs, check that each one allows the traffic in its own order.

concepts.heading: Service Tags
concepts.body: A service tag is a named group of IP prefixes that Microsoft maintains, used as a source or destination in NSG rules instead of address lists. Common tags are VirtualNetwork, which covers the virtual network's address space, peered networks and connected on-premises ranges; Internet, which covers public address space including Azure's public endpoints; AzureLoadBalancer, which stands for the health probe source; and service tags such as Storage or Sql, many with regional versions such as Storage.WestUS. To let VMs reach only storage in their region while blocking the internet, create an allow rule for Storage.WestUS with a lower number than a deny rule for Internet; otherwise the Internet deny also blocks storage. Remember that a service tag covers every account of that service in the region, including other customers' accounts. When a question asks to allow an Azure service without maintaining IP lists, choose a service tag.

concepts.heading: Application Security Groups
concepts.body: An application security group lets NSG rules target a role instead of IP addresses. You create groups such as asg-web and asg-db, add each VM's network interface to the right group, and write rules such as source asg-web, destination asg-db, port 1433, allow. When the web tier scales from two to six VMs, you only add the new NICs to asg-web, and no rule changes. ASGs have limits: every network interface in an application security group must be in the same virtual network as the first one added, and peering does not change that, and the source and destination groups in one rule must also be in the same virtual network. When a question complains that rules break every time servers are added or their IPs change, the answer is application security groups.

concepts.heading: Azure Bastion Requirements and SKUs
concepts.body: Azure Bastion gives RDP and SSH to VMs over TLS on port 443 from the Azure portal, and connects to the VMs on their private IPs, so the VMs need no public IP. Dedicated SKUs need a subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, /26 or larger, with nothing else in it, and, except for Premium private-only deployments, a Standard public IP. The Developer SKU is free and shared, connects to one VM at a time and suits dev/test. Basic gives a dedicated host with browser connections. Standard adds host scaling, native client support through commands such as az network bastion ssh, shareable links, IP-based connection, custom ports and file transfer. Premium adds session recording and private-only deployment without a public IP. You can upgrade a SKU but not downgrade. When a question needs a local SSH client or file transfer, pick Standard; for recorded sessions, Premium.

concepts.heading: NSGs and Bastion Sessions
concepts.body: A Bastion session has two legs. Users reach the bastion host on port 443, and the bastion host reaches the target VM on 3389 or 22 over the private network. An NSG on AzureBastionSubnet is optional, but if you add one it must contain all the required rules, such as inbound 443 from Internet and from GatewayManager; RDP and SSH ports are not needed inbound there. The NSG on the target VM's subnet or NIC must allow RDP or SSH inbound from the AzureBastionSubnet address range, numbered ahead of any custom deny rule. For example, with AzureBastionSubnet 10.0.254.0/26, an allow rule at priority 100 for source 10.0.254.0/26, port 3389, fixes a session that times out after a deny-all at 200. When Bastion connects to some VMs but not others, compare the target subnets' NSGs.

examPoints: A question where an allow rule seems ignored is testing that NSG rules are processed by lowest priority number and stop at the first match, across both subnet and NIC NSGs.
A question about writing NSG rules that survive scaling a tier is testing application security groups, which work only within one virtual network.
A question that asks for SSH with a local client, file transfer or session recording through Azure Bastion is testing the Standard and Premium SKU features.

quiz.q: An NSG on snet-web has a custom rule DenyAllInbound at priority 200 and a new rule AllowHttps at priority 300 for TCP 443 from Internet. Users still cannot reach the web VMs on 443. What is the fix?
choices: Move AllowHttps to the outbound direction, because NSGs check responses before requests for HTTPS traffic
Delete the default rule DenyAllInBound at priority 65500, which overrides custom allow rules for internet sources
Associate the same NSG with each web VM's network interface so that the subnet and NIC rules are merged
Change AllowHttps to a priority number below 200 so it is evaluated before the deny rule matches the traffic
quiz.explain: NSG rules run from the lowest number up and stop at the first match, so the deny at 200 wins until the allow has a lower number. Choice B is tempting because DenyAllInBound is a real default rule, but default rules cannot be deleted and are evaluated only after all custom rules.

quiz.q: Security wants administrators to connect to Linux VMs through Azure Bastion from their own terminal with a local SSH client, and the VMs must have no public IPs. Which Bastion SKU is the lowest that meets the need?
choices: Developer, because it is free and supports native SSH clients for one VM at a time on shared infrastructure
Standard, because native client support starts at Standard and works with az network bastion ssh
Basic, because its dedicated host with two instances supports local clients as well as browser sessions
Premium, because every native client connection must be recorded and only Premium supports recording
quiz.explain: Native client support, which lets users connect with their own SSH or RDP client, is available on Standard and Premium. Choice D is tempting because Premium also supports native client, but it is not the lowest SKU that meets the need, and recording applies to browser sessions, not native client ones.

days.recap: NSG rules stop at the first match by priority, both subnet and NIC NSGs must allow a flow, service tags and ASGs replace IP lists, and Bastion needs AzureBastionSubnet plus the right SKU and target NSG rules.

days.title: Service Endpoints, Private Endpoints, and Private DNS

concepts.heading: Service Endpoints
concepts.body: A service endpoint is a subnet setting, for example Microsoft.Storage on snet-app. Traffic from that subnet still goes to the service's public endpoint, but over the Azure backbone and with the subnet's identity, so the storage account sees the VM's private address and subnet instead of a public IP. That has a side effect: an IP firewall rule for the old public address stops matching, so you add a virtual network rule that allows the subnet on the storage account. DNS does not change, and the service still resolves to a public IP. Service endpoints only serve traffic that starts in that Azure subnet; they never help on-premises clients. When a question says storage access broke right after a service endpoint was enabled, the fix is a virtual network rule for the subnet, not a new IP rule.

concepts.heading: Service Endpoint Policies
concepts.body: A service tag or a service endpoint lets a subnet reach every storage account in a region, including accounts that belong to someone else, which leaves a data exfiltration gap. A service endpoint policy closes it. You attach the policy to a subnet that has the Azure Storage service endpoint enabled, and it acts as an allow list of resource IDs: a whole subscription, a resource group or single storage accounts. Once the policy is on the subnet, only the listed accounts are reachable over the endpoint, and every other storage account is denied. List every dependency your applications need, because anything missing is blocked, and note that policies do not apply to traffic from on-premises. When a question asks to stop VMs from copying data to storage accounts outside the company while keeping service endpoints, choose a service endpoint policy rather than an NSG service tag.

concepts.heading: Private Endpoints
concepts.body: A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP from your subnet, mapped to one resource and one target subresource, such as blob or file on a storage account. Clients reach the service on that private IP, from the same virtual network, from peered networks and from on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute, which service endpoints cannot do. Each storage service needs its own endpoint: a Data Lake Storage account needs both a blob and a dfs endpoint. The connection must be Approved before it carries traffic, and the endpoint's NIC is created for you and keeps its IP for the endpoint's lifetime. By default NSGs and route tables are not applied to traffic to private endpoints; you turn on network policies for private endpoints on the subnet to filter it. Microsoft recommends private endpoints for private access to Azure services.

concepts.heading: Private DNS Zones for Private Endpoints
concepts.body: Clients keep using normal names such as stcontoso.blob.core.windows.net, so DNS must return the private IP. Public DNS answers with a CNAME into a privatelink zone, for example stcontoso.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, and a private DNS zone named privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, linked to the virtual network, returns the endpoint's private address. Each service has its own zone, such as privatelink.file.core.windows.net. VMs using Azure-provided DNS resolve this automatically once the zone is linked. On-premises clients need a conditional forwarder for blob.core.windows.net, the public zone and not the privatelink one, to a DNS forwarder or Azure DNS Private Resolver in a virtual network linked to the zone. When nslookup from a VM returns a public IP for a storage account with a private endpoint, the zone link or the zone record is missing.

concepts.heading: Disabling Public Network Access
concepts.body: A private endpoint adds a private path but does not close the public one. To make a storage account reachable only privately, set Public network access to Disabled on the account's Networking page. All public traffic is then blocked, including from networks you once allowed through firewall rules or service endpoints, while traffic through an approved private endpoint is always allowed. The other option, Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, keeps the public endpoint open to listed subnets and addresses, which suits service endpoints. For example, a finance team that wants its storage reachable from the office over ExpressRoute and nowhere else uses a private endpoint plus Disabled. When a question asks to make sure no traffic reaches the service over its public endpoint, the answer includes disabling public network access, not only adding a private endpoint.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between the Two
concepts.body: Use a service endpoint when VMs in Azure subnets need a simple way, with no extra resource to deploy, to reach a service's public endpoint with their subnet identity, and the service's firewall should allow only those subnets. Use a private endpoint when you need a private IP for the service, access from peered networks or on-premises, protection against exfiltration to other accounts of the same service, or the public endpoint turned off entirely. Private endpoints need DNS planning with privatelink zones; service endpoints need no DNS changes but leave the service on its public address. For example, a lab VM writing logs to one account can use a service endpoint, while a branch office reaching a file share over VPN needs a private endpoint. Questions usually hinge on one word: on-premises, private IP or disable public access points to private endpoints.

examPoints: A question where storage access fails right after enabling a service endpoint is testing that the source becomes the subnet, so a virtual network rule replaces the IP rule.
A question about reaching a storage account privately from on-premises is testing private endpoints with DNS forwarding, plus disabling public network access.
A question about letting a subnet reach only the company's own storage accounts is testing service endpoint policies.

quiz.q: A storage account has a private endpoint for blob in vnet-data. A VM in vnet-data runs nslookup for the account name and gets a public IP address. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The storage account still allows public network access, which makes DNS prefer the public address over the private one
The private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net is missing or not linked to vnet-data
The subnet of the private endpoint has network policies disabled, which hides the endpoint from DNS queries
The VM's subnet lacks a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint, which is required before a private endpoint resolves
quiz.explain: The public CNAME points to the privatelink name, and only a private DNS zone linked to the network returns the private IP. Choice A is tempting because public access is a real setting to turn off, but it controls who may connect, not which address DNS returns.

quiz.q: An on-premises application must reach an Azure file share over a site-to-site VPN, and security requires that the share is not reachable over its public endpoint. Which design meets both needs?
choices: A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the gateway subnet, with a virtual network rule on the storage account
A service endpoint policy listing the storage account, attached to the subnet that holds the VPN gateway
A private endpoint for the file subresource, DNS forwarding for on-premises, and public network access disabled
An NSG on the storage account that allows only the on-premises address range on port 445 from the VPN
quiz.explain: Private endpoints are reachable from on-premises over VPN, and disabling public network access closes the public path. Choice A is tempting because service endpoints secure storage to subnets, but they only cover traffic that starts in Azure subnets, so on-premises clients would still reach the share over its public endpoint.

days.recap: Service endpoints keep the public endpoint but change the source to the subnet; private endpoints give a private IP reachable from peers and on-premises, need privatelink DNS zones, and pair with disabled public network access.

days.title: Azure DNS and Azure Load Balancer

concepts.heading: Public DNS Zones and Delegation
concepts.body: A public DNS zone in Azure DNS, such as contoso.com, hosts your records on four Azure name servers listed on the zone's overview page. Creating the zone is only half the job: the internet finds it only after you change the domain's NS records at the registrar to those four name servers, which is called delegation. A child zone such as eu.contoso.com works the same way inside Azure: the parent zone needs an NS record set named eu that lists the child zone's name servers. You can check the result with nslookup -type=NS against a public resolver. In Azure DNS the record set, a name plus a type, is the unit you manage, with one TTL per set. When a newly created zone answers in the portal but not on the internet, the missing step is delegation at the registrar or in the parent zone.

concepts.heading: Alias Record Sets
concepts.body: Two problems meet at the zone apex, the bare domain written as @. A CNAME is not allowed there, because the apex already holds NS and SOA records, and a plain A record holds a fixed address that can dangle if the public IP is deleted and later handed to someone else. An alias record set solves both. It is an A, AAAA or CNAME record set that references an Azure resource, such as a Standard public IP, a Traffic Manager profile, an Azure Front Door endpoint or another record set in the zone, instead of literal data. It follows the resource when its address changes and becomes empty if the resource is deleted, and alias A records can sit at the apex. In the portal you choose Alias record set: Yes and pick the resource. Apex-to-Azure-resource questions point to alias records.

concepts.heading: Private DNS Zones and Autoregistration
concepts.body: A private DNS zone, such as corp.contoso.net, answers only virtual networks linked to it through virtual network links. With autoregistration enabled on a link, Azure keeps an A record for each VM's primary network interface, taken from the Azure DHCP configuration of the NIC, and removes it when the VM is deleted or stopped. A virtual network can have only one registration zone, other resources such as load balancers need manual records, and a static IP or name typed inside the guest operating system is ignored, so set static private IPs on the NIC. Azure-provided DNS at 168.63.129.16 resolves linked zones. If the virtual network uses custom DNS servers such as domain controllers, those servers must forward the zone's queries to 168.63.129.16 from a linked network, otherwise lookups return NXDOMAIN.

concepts.heading: Standard Load Balancer Building Blocks
concepts.body: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 and passes TCP and UDP flows to a backend pool. A public load balancer has a public IP frontend; an internal one has a private IP frontend in a subnet. Load-balancing rules map a frontend IP and port to the backend pool and port, and health probes, TCP, HTTP or HTTPS, decide which instances receive new flows. By default the load balancer spreads flows with a five-tuple hash, so one connection stays on one VM but a client's next connection may land elsewhere; Client IP session persistence keeps all of a client's connections on the same VM. Use the Standard SKU, since Basic was retired on 30 September 2025. Standard is secure by default, so backends receive client traffic only when an NSG allows it. Questions about sticky users point to session persistence, not a new SKU.

concepts.heading: HA Ports and Outbound Rules
concepts.body: An HA ports rule is a load-balancing rule with protocol All and port 0. On an internal Standard Load Balancer it balances every TCP and UDP flow on every port with one rule, which makes it the standard way to put a highly available frontend IP in front of firewall appliances that a user-defined route points to. Public load balancers do not support it. Outbound connectivity is a separate topic: backend VMs without their own public IP reach the internet through the frontend by SNAT. An outbound rule defines that explicitly, with which frontend IP or prefix, how many SNAT ports per VM and the idle timeout. To use a different address for outbound traffic, add a frontend for it, create an outbound rule and disable outbound SNAT on the load-balancing rule. For large outbound volumes Learn recommends Azure NAT Gateway.

concepts.heading: Load Balancer Troubleshooting
concepts.body: Health probes come from 168.63.129.16, shown in NSGs as the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. A custom deny-all at a low priority number blocks probes before the default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule at 65001 is reached, every instance is marked down and no new flows are sent; fix it with an allow rule for AzureLoadBalancer on the probe port above the deny. The reverse symptom, healthy probes but clients timing out, means the NSG lacks an allow rule for the real client sources, because the AzureLoadBalancer tag covers probes only. HTTP probes need a 200 response from the probe path, so a redirect fails them. A VM in an internal load balancer's backend pool cannot reach that load balancer's own frontend. Check the Health Probe Status metric in Azure Monitor first when traffic stops.

examPoints: A question where a new Azure DNS zone does not resolve on the internet is testing delegation: the registrar's NS records, or an NS record set in the parent zone, must point to the zone's name servers.
A question about pointing the bare domain at a public IP or Front Door endpoint is testing alias record sets at the apex.
A question where all load balancer backends show unhealthy after a new NSG rule is testing that probes come from AzureLoadBalancer (168.63.129.16) and need an allow rule ahead of any deny.

quiz.q: After a security team adds an NSG rule DenyAll at priority 200 on the backend subnet, a Standard Load Balancer stops sending traffic and every backend shows unhealthy. What should the administrator add?
choices: An inbound allow rule at priority 150 for source service tag AzureLoadBalancer on the probe port
An inbound allow rule at priority 4000 for source service tag AzureLoadBalancer on the probe port
An outbound allow rule at priority 150 for destination service tag Internet on the load-balanced port
A second health probe on a different port so that the load balancer can still detect healthy instances
quiz.explain: Health probes from 168.63.129.16 are matched by the deny at 200 first, so the allow must have a lower number. Choice B names the right tag, but priority 4000 is evaluated after the deny at 200, so the probes would still be blocked.

quiz.q: A company hosts contoso.com in Azure DNS and wants the bare domain to point at a Standard public IP of a web front end, with the record updating if the IP resource changes. What should the administrator create?
choices: A CNAME record at @ that points to the DNS name label of the public IP address resource
An NS record set at @ that delegates the apex to the name servers of the public IP address
An A record at @ with the current address, refreshed by an Azure Automation runbook each night
An alias A record set at @ that references the public IP address resource in the subscription
quiz.explain: Alias A record sets are allowed at the apex and follow the referenced Azure resource. Choice A is tempting because CNAMEs point names at other names, but a CNAME is not allowed at the zone apex next to the NS and SOA records.

days.recap: Delegate public zones at the registrar or parent, use alias records at the apex, link private zones and let autoregistration track NICs, and troubleshoot Standard Load Balancer through probes, NSGs and session persistence.

days.title: Domain 4 Review: Virtual Networking

concepts.heading: Review: Address Plans and Peering
concepts.body: Start the review with the numbers. Every subnet loses five addresses, so usable addresses are 2 to the power (32 minus prefix) minus 5, and /29 is the smallest IPv4 subnet. Address spaces must not overlap with peers or on-premises ranges. Peering is two links, Initiated until both exist and Connected after, and it is not transitive, so spokes need a direct peering or an appliance in the hub. Gateway transit needs Allow gateway transit on the side that owns the gateway and Use remote gateways on the other, and a network can use only one gateway. After resizing a peered network, sync the peering. Special subnets have fixed names, GatewaySubnet and AzureBastionSubnet, and delegated subnets belong to one service. If any of these rules still feels shaky, reread day 20 and redo its quiz.

concepts.heading: Review: Routing and Public IPs
concepts.body: Routing questions follow one algorithm: longest prefix match first, and for equal prefixes user-defined beats BGP beats system. A firewall in the path needs a user-defined route with next hop Virtual appliance, IP forwarding on its Azure NIC and forwarding in its OS. Effective routes show all routes on a running VM's NIC, next hop shows the single route a packet takes, and next hop None with System Route means no peering or range matched. Public IPs are Standard and static, secure by default and zone-fixed at creation, and a public IP prefix gives a contiguous block that cannot be resized. Basic public IPs and Basic Load Balancer are retired and are never the right answer. When reading a routing scenario, write down the destination and each candidate prefix before choosing.

concepts.heading: Review: Filtering and Remote Access
concepts.body: NSG rules run from 100 to 4096 by lowest number first and stop at the first match; default rules at 65000 and above come last and cannot be deleted. Inbound traffic passes the subnet NSG then the NIC NSG, outbound the reverse, and both must allow. Service tags replace IP lists, with Internet including Azure public endpoints and AzureLoadBalancer covering probes only. Application security groups group NICs by role inside one virtual network. IP flow verify tests one NIC at a time and names the deciding rule; effective security rules need the VM running. Azure Bastion needs AzureBastionSubnet of /26 or larger and a Standard public IP on dedicated SKUs; native client and file transfer start at Standard, session recording and private-only deployment need Premium, and target subnets must allow RDP or SSH from the Bastion subnet.

concepts.heading: Review: Private Access and DNS
concepts.body: Service endpoints change the source to the subnet, need a virtual network rule on the service, and work only from Azure subnets; service endpoint policies limit a subnet to listed storage accounts. Private endpoints give one resource and subresource a private IP reachable from peers and on-premises, need privatelink DNS zones such as privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, and pair with Public network access set to Disabled. On-premises resolvers forward the public zone name to a resolver in a linked network. Public Azure DNS zones need delegation at the registrar, child zones need an NS record set in the parent, and alias record sets point the apex at Azure resources. Private zones need virtual network links, autoregistration tracks the NIC's Azure IP, and custom DNS servers must forward to 168.63.129.16.

concepts.heading: Review: Load Balancing
concepts.body: A Standard Load Balancer has frontends, backend pools, rules and health probes, spreads flows with a five-tuple hash and needs Client IP session persistence to keep a client on one VM. It is secure by default, so NSGs must allow both the probes from AzureLoadBalancer and the real client sources. HA ports, protocol All and port 0, exist only on internal load balancers and front firewall appliances. Outbound rules define SNAT explicitly; disable outbound SNAT on the load-balancing rule when you use them. Classic failures are a deny-all that blocks probes, an HTTP probe path that redirects, asymmetric routing when a default route sends replies through a firewall, and a backend VM calling its own internal load balancer's frontend. Take a 20-question D4 set in the question bank and log every miss by rule, not by question.

examPoints: A review question that mixes peering, routing and NSG symptoms is testing whether you can tell a missing route (next hop, effective routes) from a blocking rule (IP flow verify, effective security rules).
A review question about private access is testing the split between service endpoints (subnet identity, Azure-only) and private endpoints (private IP, on-premises, privatelink DNS).
A review question about load balancer health is testing the AzureLoadBalancer tag, NSG priorities and probe responses.

quiz.q: A route table on the hub's GatewaySubnet sends 10.0.0.0/8 to a firewall, but traffic from on-premises to a peered spoke at 10.1.0.0/16 bypasses the firewall. Why?
choices: The peering adds a 10.1.0.0/16 system route, and the longer prefix wins over the 10.0.0.0/8 user-defined route
User-defined routes are ignored on GatewaySubnet, so the gateway always uses only its system routes for spokes
The firewall's network interface has IP forwarding disabled, so Azure skips the route and sends traffic directly
Gateway transit is disabled on the hub peering, which makes the gateway ignore all routes to that spoke network
quiz.explain: Azure picks the longest prefix match first, so the peering's /16 system route beats the /8 user route; a /16 user route to the firewall fixes it. Choice C is tempting because IP forwarding is a real requirement for appliances, but disabled forwarding drops packets at the firewall rather than changing which route Azure selects.

quiz.q: A team needs a storage account that is reachable only from a peered spoke network and from on-premises over ExpressRoute, with no access over the public endpoint. Which pair of settings is required?
choices: A service endpoint on each spoke subnet and a virtual network rule on the storage account for each subnet
A service endpoint policy on the hub subnet and a storage firewall rule that allows the on-premises ranges
A private endpoint with a linked privatelink DNS zone, and Public network access set to Disabled
An NSG with the Storage service tag on each subnet and a deny rule for the Internet service tag below it
quiz.explain: A private endpoint is reachable from peered networks and on-premises, and disabling public network access removes the public path. Choice A is tempting because it secures storage to subnets, but service endpoints serve only traffic that starts in those Azure subnets, not on-premises clients.

days.recap: Domain 4 comes down to address math, peering rules, longest-prefix routing, NSG priority order, private versus service endpoints with their DNS, and Standard Load Balancer probes and rules.

days.title: Metrics, Logs, Diagnostic Settings, and KQL

concepts.heading: Three Kinds of Platform Data
concepts.body: Azure resources produce platform data with different defaults. Platform metrics, such as a VM's Percentage CPU, are collected automatically. The activity log is also automatic: it records control-plane operations such as creating, changing or deleting resources and role assignments, with the caller, and keeps them for 90 days. Resource logs record data-plane operations inside a resource, such as a SecretGet on a key vault or a request to a database, and they are not collected until you create a diagnostic setting. Guest operating system data, such as memory used or Windows event logs, needs an agent. So when a question asks who deleted a VM, look in the activity log; when it asks who read a secret, you need key vault resource logs, and those exist only from the moment the diagnostic setting was created.

concepts.heading: Metrics Explorer: Aggregation and Dimensions
concepts.body: Metrics Explorer plots platform metrics by grouping raw values into time grains and reducing each grain with an aggregation: Avg, Max, Min, Sum or Count. Larger grains smooth spikes, so a VM that hits 100 percent CPU for two minutes still averages near 20 percent over a six-hour grain; to find short peaks, choose Max with a small granularity such as 1 or 5 minutes. The smallest grain is 1 minute. Many metrics have dimensions: a storage account's Transactions metric can be filtered to ResponseType values that are errors and then split by API name to see which operation fails. You can pin charts to dashboards and create alert rules from them. When a question says the chart looks normal but users report brief slowdowns, the answer is a different aggregation or granularity, not a new data source.

concepts.heading: Diagnostic Settings and Their Destinations
concepts.body: A diagnostic setting on a resource selects log categories, or category groups such as audit or allLogs, and metrics, and sends them to destinations. A Log Analytics workspace is for KQL analysis, alerts and workbooks. A storage account is for low-cost archive and can use an immutability policy. An event hub streams data to external tools such as a non-Microsoft SIEM. Partner solutions cover specific integrations. A resource can have up to five settings, one destination of each type per setting, and storage accounts and event hubs must be in the same region as a regional resource. The activity log has its own diagnostic setting, under Export Activity Logs, which sends entries to the AzureActivity table for retention beyond 90 days. Questions that list a need, such as analyze, archive or stream, map directly to workspace, storage or event hub.

concepts.heading: Azure Monitor Agent and Data Collection Rules
concepts.body: Guest data comes from the Azure Monitor Agent, installed as the AzureMonitorWindowsAgent or AzureMonitorLinuxAgent extension. What it collects is defined in data collection rules: each DCR lists data sources, such as performance counters, Windows event logs, Syslog or text logs, and destinations such as a Log Analytics workspace. You associate DCRs with machines, and one agent can use many DCRs. A DCR must be in the same region as its workspace destinations, so workspaces in two regions need two DCRs. When you create a DCR in the portal and add VMs, the portal installs the agent and creates the associations for you. The Log Analytics agent was retired in August 2024 and the Azure Diagnostics extension in March 2026, so neither is ever the answer. For Arc-enabled on-premises servers, the same agent and DCRs apply.

concepts.heading: Log Analytics Workspaces and Access Modes
concepts.body: A Log Analytics workspace stores log data in tables such as AzureActivity, Perf, Event, Syslog and resource-specific tables, each with retention settings. Where you open Logs decides what a query can see. Workspace-context, opened from the workspace, covers all data in the tables you are allowed to read. Resource-context, opened from a VM, resource group or subscription, covers only records tied to that scope through the _ResourceId column, in any workspace. The workspace's access control mode decides how permissions are checked: with Use resource or workspace permissions, a developer who has Reader on one VM can query that VM's logs from the VM's Logs blade without any role on the workspace. Questions about giving application teams their own logs from a shared workspace point to resource-context access, not a separate workspace per team.

concepts.heading: KQL Basics for Administrators
concepts.body: Kusto Query Language reads like a pipeline: start with a table and pass rows through operators separated by the pipe character. where filters rows, and the time filter belongs right after the table, for example where TimeGenerated > ago(7d). summarize groups and aggregates, such as summarize count() by Computer or avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h); bin rounds timestamps so you get one point per hour instead of one per record. project chooses columns, top and order by sort, and render timechart draws a line chart and must be the last operator. A full example: Perf | where CounterName == "Available MBytes" | summarize avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | render timechart. For audits, AzureActivity | where OperationNameValue has "roleAssignments" lists role changes. Exam items test reading a query and spotting the missing bin or misplaced render.

examPoints: A question about who read a secret or which data-plane requests failed is testing resource logs, which need a diagnostic setting before any data exists.
A question about collecting memory or event logs from VMs is testing the Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules, never the retired Log Analytics agent.
A question that shows a KQL query with one row per record instead of a trend is testing summarize by bin(TimeGenerated, ...) and render as the last operator.

quiz.q: Auditors ask which users retrieved secrets from kv-prod last month. The key vault has no diagnostic settings. What can the administrator provide?
choices: The SecretGet entries in the subscription's activity log, which records every data-plane operation for 90 days
The key vault's Service API Hit metric split by caller, which shows each user who retrieved a secret
A KQL query on the AzureDiagnostics table in the default workspace, which every key vault writes to automatically
Nothing for last month; create a diagnostic setting for the AuditEvent category so future retrievals are recorded
quiz.explain: Resource logs such as AuditEvent are collected only after a diagnostic setting exists, so past secret reads are not recorded anywhere. Choice A is tempting because the activity log is automatic, but it records control-plane operations such as changing the vault, not data-plane reads of secrets.

quiz.q: A Windows VM needs its Application and System event logs collected into law-ops. Which approach should the administrator use?
choices: Install the Log Analytics agent and connect it to law-ops through the workspace's legacy agents page
Install the Azure Monitor Agent and associate a data collection rule that sends those event logs to law-ops
Create a diagnostic setting on the VM resource that sends the Windows event log category to law-ops
Enable VM insights on the VM, which sends every Windows event log to law-ops without any further rule
quiz.explain: Guest data is collected by the Azure Monitor Agent according to data collection rules. Choice C is tempting because diagnostic settings route platform logs, but a VM's diagnostic setting covers host metrics, not the guest operating system's event logs.

days.recap: Metrics and the activity log are automatic, resource logs need diagnostic settings, guest data needs the Azure Monitor Agent with DCRs, access mode decides what a Logs query sees, and KQL trends need summarize by bin and a final render.

days.title: Alerts, Insights, and Network Watcher Monitoring

concepts.heading: Alert Rule Types
concepts.body: An alert rule watches a signal and fires when its condition is met. Metric alerts evaluate numeric metrics, such as Percentage CPU above 80 for 15 minutes, and can watch many resources of one type in a region with one rule. Log search alerts run a KQL query against a workspace on a schedule and fire on the number of rows or a measured value; they can split by a column such as _ResourceId to raise one alert per resource. Activity log alerts fire when a specific control-plane event is written, such as a VM being deleted or restarted, with no agent or workspace. Service Health alerts cover Azure-side incidents and planned maintenance for your services and regions. The deciding question is where the signal lives: a number, a query result or an event in the activity log.

concepts.heading: Action Groups
concepts.body: An action group is a reusable list of who to notify and what to run when an alert fires. Notification types include email, SMS, push to the Azure mobile app and voice. Action types include Azure Functions, Logic Apps, Automation runbooks, webhooks and ITSM connections. One action group can serve many alert rules, so changing the on-call address happens in one place. A useful option is Email Azure Resource Manager role: it emails whoever holds a subscription role such as Owner, Contributor, Reader, Monitoring Contributor or Monitoring Reader, so new team members are notified without editing the group. For example, ag-ops-email might email the Owner role and call a runbook that collects diagnostics. When a question asks how to notify everyone with a role, or reuse the same notifications across rules, the answer is an action group setting.

concepts.heading: Alert Processing Rules
concepts.body: An alert rule decides when an alert fires; an alert processing rule changes what happens to alerts that have already fired. It has a scope, a subscription, resource group or specific resources with optional filters such as severity or alert rule, an action and a schedule. The Suppression action removes notifications from matching alerts, which still fire and appear in the alerts list; Apply action groups adds action groups to matching alerts, including alerts that no alert rule created, such as Azure Backup alerts. Schedules can be always, one-time or recurring, such as Saturday 22:00 to Sunday 02:00 each week. Learn says a new or changed rule can take up to 30 minutes to take effect, so create it well before the window. When a question wants silence during maintenance without disabling every rule, or one action group added across many alerts, choose an alert processing rule.

concepts.heading: Azure Monitor Insights
concepts.body: Insights are ready-made monitoring experiences, built on workbooks, for a type of resource. VM insights shows performance trends for VMs and scale sets using data that the Azure Monitor Agent sends to a workspace. Storage insights gives a view across many storage accounts and subscriptions of availability, transactions, latency and capacity, with drill-down per account; it uses the platform metrics every account emits, so nothing needs to be enabled. Network insights shows the health and topology of network resources, and Key Vault insights covers vault requests and failures. Insights can be customized and saved as your own workbook. When a question asks to compare many storage accounts' availability and capacity quickly, or to see VM performance trends across a fleet, choose the matching insight rather than building custom dashboards or queries.

concepts.heading: Virtual Network Flow Logs and Traffic Analytics
concepts.body: Network Watcher flow logs record the IP flows through your network. Virtual network flow logs are enabled on a virtual network, subnet or network interface and record each flow's five-tuple, direction, whether it was allowed or denied, throughput and the rule that decided it. Records go as JSON to a storage account in the same region. Network security group flow logs are retiring on 30 September 2027 and new ones can no longer be created, so new designs use virtual network flow logs. Traffic analytics reads the flow logs, aggregates and enriches them with geography and topology, and stores the result in a Log Analytics workspace, showing hot spots, open ports and traffic across regions and the internet. When a question asks to record all traffic in a network for audit or to visualize traffic patterns, answer virtual network flow logs plus traffic analytics.

concepts.heading: Connection Troubleshoot Versus Connection Monitor
concepts.body: Network Watcher has one-time tools and one ongoing tool. Connection troubleshoot runs a single TCP or ICMP test from a VM, scale set, Bastion host or application gateway to a VM, FQDN, URI or IP and reports reachability, latency and the hops, which suits an incident happening now. Connection monitor runs checks over TCP, HTTP or ICMP at a set frequency from sources such as VMs or Arc-enabled on-premises machines to destinations such as VMs, URLs or IP addresses, stores results in Log Analytics, emits Checks Failed and round-trip time metrics and supports alerts. For example, a test group from three app VMs to 10.20.5.10 on TCP 443 every 60 seconds can alert when more than 5 percent of checks fail. When a question needs history, trends or alerts on reachability, choose Connection monitor; for a one-off check, Connection troubleshoot.

examPoints: A question about being told when someone deletes or restarts a resource is testing activity log alerts, while thresholds point to metric alerts and KQL conditions to log search alerts.
A question about silencing notifications during a maintenance window, or adding an action group to many alerts at once, is testing alert processing rules.
A question about recording every flow in a virtual network is testing virtual network flow logs with traffic analytics, since NSG flow logs can no longer be created.

quiz.q: Operations wants no alert emails for rg-erp every Saturday from 22:00 to 02:00 during patching, but the alerts must still appear in the portal. What should the administrator configure?
choices: An alert processing rule scoped to rg-erp with the Suppression action and a weekly recurring schedule
A script that disables every alert rule in rg-erp on Saturday night and enables them again on Sunday
A CanNotDelete lock on the action group during the window so that it cannot send notifications
A second action group with no recipients, assigned to every alert rule in rg-erp for the weekend
quiz.explain: Suppression in an alert processing rule removes notifications while the alerts still fire and remain visible, on a recurring schedule. Choice B is tempting because it stops the emails, but disabled rules raise no alerts at all, so nothing would appear in the portal.

quiz.q: A network team needs reachability and latency between three app VMs and an on-premises server recorded every minute for weeks, with an alert when checks start failing. Which tool fits?
choices: Connection troubleshoot, scheduled through an Automation runbook to run every minute and email results
IP flow verify on each app VM's network interface, run against the on-premises address and port
Virtual network flow logs with traffic analytics, filtered to the on-premises server's address range
Connection monitor with a test group from the three VMs to the server, and an alert on Checks Failed
quiz.explain: Connection monitor runs checks at regular intervals, keeps history and exposes metrics for alerts. Choice C is tempting because flow logs record traffic to that server, but they show flows that happened, not active reachability tests or round-trip latency.

days.recap: Choose the alert type by where the signal lives, reuse action groups, use alert processing rules for suppression and bulk routing, prefer insights for ready-made views, and use virtual network flow logs and Connection monitor for network evidence over time.

days.title: Azure Backup: Vaults, Policies, and Restores

concepts.heading: Recovery Services Vault Versus Backup Vault
concepts.body: Azure Backup keeps recovery points and policies in a vault, and the workload decides which type. A Recovery Services vault protects Azure VMs, SQL Server and SAP HANA databases in Azure VMs, Azure Files shares and on-premises machines through the MARS agent or Azure Backup Server, and it is also the vault Azure Site Recovery uses. A Backup vault protects newer data sources such as Azure managed disks with Azure Disk Backup, Azure Blobs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Kubernetes Service. The two have separate policies and items; you cannot point a disk backup at a Recovery Services vault. Both can be used side by side, for example daily VM backup in one and hourly disk snapshots in the other. For VM backup, the vault must be in the same region as the VM. Vault-choice questions are answered by the data source alone.

concepts.heading: Vault Redundancy and Cross Region Restore
concepts.body: A vault's backup storage redundancy, LRS, ZRS or GRS, must be set before the first item is protected; afterwards the only way to change it is to protect the items again in a new vault. GRS copies backup data to the paired region, but by default you can restore from that copy only after Microsoft declares an outage in the primary region. Cross Region Restore, a vault property on GRS vaults, makes the secondary copy restorable whenever you choose, for drills or audits; once protection has started it cannot be turned back off. In the secondary region you can create a VM or restore disks from vault-tier recovery points. For example, an auditor's request to prove restores in the paired region needs Cross Region Restore enabled, not just GRS. Remember that region pairing alone never fails anything over automatically.

concepts.heading: Soft Delete and Immutable Vaults
concepts.body: Soft delete keeps deleted backup data for 14 days by default at no extra cost, and the period can be extended. New vaults have it on by default, and it also covers recovery points removed by backup policy changes. To recover, select the soft-deleted item and choose Undelete; the item returns to Stop protection with retain data, and you can then restore or resume backups. An immutable vault blocks operations that lose recovery points, such as stopping protection with deletion of data or reducing retention in a policy, while increasing retention stays possible. It has three states: Disabled, Enabled, which an authorized user can turn off, and Enabled and locked, which is irreversible. Microsoft recommends testing in the Enabled state before locking. When a question says nobody, even an administrator, may shorten or delete backups, ever, the answer is a locked immutable vault.

concepts.heading: VM Backup Policies
concepts.body: A backup policy sets the schedule and how long recovery points are kept, daily, weekly, monthly and yearly. Azure VM policies in a Recovery Services vault come in two types. The Standard policy takes one scheduled backup per day and keeps instant restore snapshots for 1 to 5 days. The Enhanced policy adds hourly schedules, with backups every 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24 hours, keeps instant restore snapshots for up to 30 days, and is required for VMs with Premium SSD v2 or Ultra Disks. Once a VM is protected with an Enhanced policy, you cannot move it back to a Standard policy. For example, a policy of every 4 hours from 08:00 for 24 hours creates six recovery points per day. Questions with several backups per day or newer disk types point to the Enhanced policy.

concepts.heading: Restore Options for Azure VMs
concepts.body: From a VM recovery point you can choose Create new virtual machine, which quickly builds a basic VM with a new name in the same region; Restore disks, which creates managed disks plus a generated template so you can deploy a customized VM, for example with a specific size, availability set or extra settings; Replace existing, which keeps the VM resource, its name and network interface, takes a snapshot of the current disks and swaps in the recovery point's disks; and File Recovery, which mounts the recovery point as drives through a downloaded script so you can copy single files. The machine running the File Recovery script needs outbound TCP 3260 to the recovery service. When a VM still exists but will not boot after a bad update, Replace existing is the cleanest roll back; when you need one deleted folder, use File Recovery.

concepts.heading: Azure Files Backup Tiers
concepts.body: Azure Files backup is configured in a Recovery Services vault and offers two tiers. The snapshot tier takes share snapshots that live in the same storage account as the share, so restores are fast, but if the storage account is deleted the snapshots go with it; the vault holds only metadata, and the vault redundancy setting does not apply. The vault-standard tier, also called vaulted backup, copies changed data into the vault after each snapshot, giving an offsite copy isolated from the source account, long-term retention and cross-region options. You can restore a whole share or individual files, to the original or an alternate location. When a question requires backups that survive deletion of the storage account or a ransomware attack on it, choose the vaulted tier; for quick, short-term rollbacks only, snapshots are enough.

examPoints: A question that names a data source such as a managed disk, a blob container or a VM is testing which vault type protects it: Backup vault for disks and blobs, Recovery Services vault for VMs and Azure Files.

A question about restoring in the paired region at any time is testing Cross Region Restore on a GRS vault, while one about changing redundancy after backups started is testing that it must be set first.
A question about backups that nobody can shorten or delete is testing a locked immutable vault, while one about recovering deleted backups is testing soft delete and Undelete.

quiz.q: An administrator needs hourly backups of a single Azure managed data disk, separate from the VM's daily backup. Which vault and feature should be used?
choices: The existing Recovery Services vault, by adding the disk to the VM's backup policy with an hourly schedule
A Recovery Services vault with an Enhanced policy, which backs up individual data disks without the VM
A Backup vault with Azure Disk Backup and a disk backup policy that runs on an hourly schedule
A storage account lifecycle management rule that copies the disk to a cool container every hour
quiz.explain: Azure Disk Backup protects managed disks from a Backup vault and can run several times a day alongside the VM backup. Choice B is tempting because Enhanced policies allow hourly VM backups, but they protect the whole VM in a Recovery Services vault, not a single disk on its own.

quiz.q: A VM named web01 still exists but will not boot after a faulty update last night. The team wants the same VM, name and network interface back with yesterday's disks. Which restore option fits?
choices: Create new virtual machine, using the same name web01 so that the new VM takes over the old network interface
Replace existing, which takes a snapshot of the current disks and swaps in the recovery point's disks
File Recovery, which mounts the recovery point so the team can copy the system files back into web01
Restore disks to a new resource group, then delete web01 and deploy a fresh VM from the generated template
quiz.explain: Replace existing keeps the VM resource and swaps its disks for the recovery point's disks. Choice A is tempting because it is the quickest restore, but it requires a name that does not already exist, so it builds a separate VM rather than repairing web01.

days.recap: Pick the vault by data source, set redundancy before the first backup, enable Cross Region Restore for on-demand secondary restores, rely on soft delete and locked immutability against deletion, choose Enhanced policies for several backups a day, and match the restore option to the damage.

days.title: Azure Site Recovery and Backup Monitoring

concepts.heading: Setting Up Azure VM Replication
concepts.body: Azure Site Recovery replicates VMs to another region so you can fail over during a regional outage. It uses a Recovery Services vault, and unlike Azure Backup the vault must be in a region other than the VMs' source region, usually the target region so it stays usable when the source is down. In the vault you select Enable Site Recovery, pick the source region and VMs and the target region, and Site Recovery installs the Mobility service extension on each VM. Disk writes go to a cache storage account in the source region and are replicated to the target, where recovery points are created according to the replication policy, including app-consistent points. Target resources such as the resource group and virtual network are chosen or created during setup. Region pairing alone never replicates a VM; Site Recovery or a backup does.

concepts.heading: Test Failover
concepts.body: A test failover is a disaster recovery drill. On a replicated item or a recovery plan you select Test Failover, choose a recovery point, for example Latest processed for a low recovery time, and pick a target virtual network. Microsoft recommends an isolated, non-production network so the test VMs do not clash with production addresses or services. The test creates VMs in the target region from the recovery point without affecting production or ongoing replication. After you check the application, you select Cleanup test failover, record notes and confirm testing is complete, and the test VMs are deleted. Microsoft suggests running a test failover for each application regularly, such as every quarter. When a question asks how to prove the DR plan works without downtime or interrupting replication, the answer is test failover into an isolated network, not a real failover.

concepts.heading: Failover, Commit, Re-protect, and Failback
concepts.body: A real failover creates VMs in the target region from a recovery point, optionally shutting down the source VMs first. After checking the result you commit the failover, which removes the other recovery points. The VMs now run in the secondary region unprotected. To go home, re-protect them, which reverses replication to secondary-to-primary; if the original disks still exist, only the differences are sent. Then fail over again from secondary to primary, which is the failback, and re-protect once more so replication runs primary-to-secondary as before. While the reverse replication runs, Site Recovery places a read-only lock on the original machine so it is not deleted. When a question lists these steps out of order, remember the pattern: fail over, commit, re-protect, fail back, re-protect.

concepts.heading: Recovery Plans
concepts.body: A recovery plan groups replicated machines that fail over together, usually one application. Machines in the same group fail over in parallel, and group 2 starts only after every machine in group 1 has failed over and started, so a three-tier app puts the database in group 1, middleware in group 2 and the web front end in group 3. You can add Azure Automation runbooks or scripts before or after a group, for example to assign a public IP or an NSG to the failed-over web VMs, and manual actions that pause the plan until someone confirms a step that cannot be automated. You can run a test failover on the whole plan, and choose recovery points such as Latest processed or Latest app-consistent. When a question needs a startup order or custom steps during failover, the answer is a recovery plan.

concepts.heading: Backup Alerts
concepts.body: Azure Backup raises built-in Azure Monitor alerts without setup. Security alerts, such as deletion of backup data, cannot be turned off; job failure alerts, such as backup or restore failures, are on by default and can be turned off per vault. The alerts appear in Azure Monitor and in Resiliency, the experience that extends the earlier Azure Business Continuity Center. Receiving an email is a separate step: create an alert processing rule that applies an action group to the backup alerts, because these alerts have no alert rule to attach an action group to. For custom conditions, send vault diagnostics to a Log Analytics workspace and write log search alerts. Classic alerts on the vault's Backup Alerts page are deprecated, so they are not the answer. When a question asks how to be emailed about failed backup jobs, think alert processing rule plus action group.

concepts.heading: Backup Reports
concepts.body: Backup Reports are Azure workbooks that show backup items, jobs, policies, usage and trends across vaults, subscriptions and regions. They read from Azure Monitor Logs, so each Recovery Services vault and Backup vault needs a diagnostic setting that sends its backup diagnostic data to a Log Analytics workspace; a built-in Azure Policy definition can configure this for every vault in a scope. The workspace can be in any region and subscription. The first data can take up to 24 hours to arrive, reports show only completed days, and Microsoft suggests looking two days after setup; raise the workspace retention for longer history. You then open Backup Reports from Resiliency or a vault and choose the workspace. When a report is empty right after setup, or a vault is missing from it, check the diagnostic setting and the elapsed time before anything else.

examPoints: A question about where to create the vault is testing the split: Azure Backup needs the vault in the VM's region, Site Recovery needs it outside the source region.
A question about a DR drill without downtime is testing test failover into an isolated network, while one about returning to the primary region is testing commit, re-protect and failback.
A question about emailing failed backup jobs is testing built-in Azure Monitor alerts routed by an alert processing rule to an action group.

quiz.q: A company replicates VMs from East US to West US with Site Recovery and must prove recovery works every quarter without affecting production or replication. What should the administrator run?
choices: A planned failover to West US during a maintenance window, followed by an immediate failback to East US
A restore of each VM from its latest backup recovery point into a new resource group in West US
A test failover into an isolated virtual network in West US, followed by Cleanup test failover
A re-protect operation that reverses replication so the West US copies can be started and checked
quiz.explain: Test failover builds VMs from a recovery point without touching production or replication, and cleanup removes them. Choice A is tempting because it fully exercises the plan, but a real failover moves production and interrupts the normal replication direction.

quiz.q: Backup jobs fail occasionally across 12 Recovery Services vaults, and the team wants one email each time. The built-in job failure alerts are on. What else is needed?
choices: Enable the classic alerts on each vault's Backup Alerts page and add the team address to each vault
Create an activity log alert on each vault for failed backup jobs, scoped to the vault resource
Send each vault's diagnostics to a storage account and configure a lifecycle rule that emails failures
Create an alert processing rule over the subscription that applies an action group emailing the team
quiz.explain: Built-in backup alerts have no alert rule of their own, so an alert processing rule attaches the action group that sends the email. Choice A is tempting because classic alerts once sent backup emails, but they are deprecated and Learn points to the built-in Azure Monitor alerts instead.

days.recap: Site Recovery needs a vault outside the source region, drills use test failover with cleanup, failback means commit, re-protect, fail over and re-protect again, recovery plans order tiers, and backup alerts and reports depend on processing rules and workspace diagnostics.

days.title: Domain 5 Review: Monitor and Maintain Azure Resources

concepts.heading: Review: Where Each Signal Lives
concepts.body: Most monitoring questions are answered by knowing where the data lives. Platform metrics are automatic and are charted in Metrics Explorer, where Max with a small granularity finds short spikes and splitting by a dimension shows which segment misbehaves. The activity log is automatic, records control-plane operations for 90 days, and is exported with its own diagnostic setting for longer retention or KQL. Resource logs record data-plane operations and exist only after a diagnostic setting sends them to a workspace, storage account or event hub. Guest data comes from the Azure Monitor Agent through data collection rules in the same region as the workspace. Retired agents, the Log Analytics agent and the Azure Diagnostics extension, are never correct. Before answering, ask yourself whether the scenario's data is a metric, an activity log event, a resource log or guest data.

concepts.heading: Review: Queries and Access
concepts.body: A Log Analytics workspace holds tables such as AzureActivity, Perf, Event and Syslog. Logs opened from the workspace run in workspace-context and see all tables you can read; Logs opened from a resource run in resource-context and see only that resource's records, which, with resource-or-workspace permissions, lets teams query their own VMs without workspace roles. KQL starts with a table, filters with where early, groups with summarize and bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) for trends, picks columns with project and ends with render. When reading a query in a question, check three things: is there a time filter, is the time column binned before charting, and is render the final operator. Practice by writing one query a day against your own lab workspace, such as counting Heartbeat records by Computer over the last hour.

concepts.heading: Review: Alerts and Network Evidence
concepts.body: Choose alert types by signal: metric alerts for thresholds, log search alerts for KQL results, activity log alerts for events such as deletes and restarts, and Service Health alerts for Azure incidents. Action groups hold notifications and actions, including Email Azure Resource Manager role. Alert processing rules act on fired alerts: Suppression silences notifications on a schedule while alerts still appear, and Apply action groups adds notifications across many alerts, including backup alerts. Insights give ready-made views, such as Storage insights across many accounts with no setup. For networks, virtual network flow logs record flows to same-region storage and traffic analytics visualizes them in a workspace, since new NSG flow logs cannot be created. Connection troubleshoot checks once; Connection monitor tests continuously with history and alerts. Redo days 26 and 27 quizzes if any pairing slipped.

concepts.heading: Review: Backup
concepts.body: Pick the vault by data source: Recovery Services vault for VMs, SQL and SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files and on-premises agents; Backup vault for managed disks, blobs, PostgreSQL and AKS. Set storage redundancy before the first backup, and enable Cross Region Restore on a GRS vault to restore in the paired region whenever you choose. Soft delete keeps deleted data 14 days by default and Undelete brings it back; a locked immutable vault blocks deletion and retention cuts permanently. Enhanced VM policies allow several backups a day and are required for Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks. Restore options are Create new VM, Restore disks for customized deployments, Replace existing for in-place rollback and File Recovery for single files. For Azure Files, the vaulted tier survives deletion of the storage account and snapshots do not.

concepts.heading: Review: Site Recovery and Reporting
concepts.body: Site Recovery needs a Recovery Services vault outside the source region, replicates through the Mobility service extension and a cache storage account, and creates recovery points in the target region. Drills use test failover into an isolated network and end with Cleanup test failover. A real event runs failover and commit, then re-protect, failback and re-protect again. Recovery plans fail over groups in order and add runbooks or manual steps.
