Backup monitoring relies on built-in Azure Monitor alerts routed by alert processing rules to action groups, and Backup Reports need each vault's diagnostics in a Log Analytics workspace, with the first data taking up to a day. Finish today with a 15-question D5 set from the question bank, then add every miss to your error log with the rule it tested.

examPoints: A review question that mixes monitoring tools is testing whether you can map a need to its signal: metric, activity log, resource log via diagnostic setting, or guest data via the Azure Monitor Agent.
A review question about protection choices is testing vault type, redundancy timing, Cross Region Restore, soft delete versus immutability, and Backup versus Site Recovery vault placement.

quiz.q: A manager wants an email whenever anyone deletes a resource group in the production subscription. Which alert rule type should the administrator create?
choices: A metric alert on the subscription's resource count metric with a threshold of one fewer than today
An activity log alert for the resource group delete operation, scoped to the subscription, with an action group
A log search alert on the Perf table that counts resource groups every five minutes and fires on a drop
A Service Health alert for the subscription that fires on any change in the list of resource groups
quiz.explain: Deleting a resource group is a control-plane operation recorded in the activity log, so an activity log alert fires on it directly. Choice C is tempting because log search alerts are flexible, but the Perf table holds guest performance counters, not resource deletions.

quiz.q: A team must restore an Azure VM in the paired region for an audit while the primary region is healthy. The vault uses GRS. What must be true?
choices: Cross Region Restore is enabled on the vault, so the secondary-region copy can be restored at any time
Microsoft has declared an outage in the primary region, which is the only time GRS data can ever be used
The vault was created in the paired region, because Azure Backup keeps the vault outside the VM's region
Site Recovery is enabled for the VM, because Azure Backup cannot restore any VM into another region
quiz.explain: Cross Region Restore makes the GRS copy restorable on demand, for drills and audits. Choice B is tempting because it describes plain GRS behavior, but Cross Region Restore exists precisely to remove that restriction.

days.recap: Domain 5 rewards matching each need to its signal and tool: metrics, activity log, resource logs and guest data for monitoring; alert types, action groups and processing rules for notification; and the right vault, policy, restore option or Site Recovery step for recovery.

days.title: Hands-On Lab Plan: One Weekend Across All Five Domains

concepts.heading: Set Up a Safe Lab
concepts.body: An administrator exam rewards hands-on memory: the blade where a setting lives, the order of steps, the error you see when something is missing. Use a subscription you control, create one resource group per lab block, such as rg-lab-net, and set a budget with an alert on the subscription before you start. Pick one region close to you and keep everything there. Stop VMs when you pause; in the portal, Stop deallocates the VM so compute charges stop, though disks and networking still bill, while shutting down from inside the guest does not. At the end of each block, delete its resource group so nothing keeps running. Keep a short lab log of each command or portal path you used. If a step fails, write down the exact error message, because exam scenarios often describe that same symptom and ask for the fix.

concepts.heading: Saturday Morning: Identity and Governance
concepts.body: Spend about two hours on Domain 1. In Microsoft Entra ID, create two test users and a security group, add a user to it, and invite a guest. Assign the group the Reader role on rg-lab-net, then use Check access on that resource group to confirm the role, and try an action as that user to see the access denied message. Assign the built-in policy that limits allowed locations to your region at the resource group, then try to create a resource in another region and read the deny reason. Add a tag policy that adds or inherits a cost-center tag, create a resource, and check the tag. Put a CanNotDelete lock on the resource group, try to delete a storage account inside it, then remove the lock. Each failure you trigger here is an exam answer.

concepts.heading: Saturday Afternoon: Storage
concepts.body: Spend about two hours on Domain 2. Create a general-purpose v2 storage account, a private container and an Azure file share. Upload a file with Storage Explorer or AzCopy, generate a service SAS for one blob, open it in a browser, then issue a second SAS tied to a stored access policy and revoke it by changing the policy. On the Networking page, switch to selected networks and watch your own client lose access until you add your IP. Enable blob soft delete and versioning, delete and overwrite a blob, and restore both. Write a lifecycle management rule that moves blobs to the Cool tier after some days of no modification. Finally, change the account's redundancy if the portal offers the conversion, and note which options it allows. Delete the resource group, or keep the account if the networking block will reuse it for a private endpoint.

concepts.heading: Sunday Morning: Compute
concepts.body: Spend about three hours on Domain 3. Deploy a small Bicep file that creates a virtual network and a VM, first with az deployment group what-if and then with az deployment group create, and read what-if's create and modify markers. Resize the VM and note which sizes need a stop. Add a data disk and initialize it inside the guest. Create an App Service plan at Standard tier or higher, deploy a web app, add a staging slot, mark one app setting as a deployment slot setting, swap, and confirm which setting stayed behind. Run a container in Azure Container Instances from a public image and read its logs. If time allows, create a small virtual machine scale set with an autoscale rule on CPU and watch instance counts in the portal. Delete what you will not reuse.

concepts.heading: Sunday Afternoon: Networking
concepts.body: Spend about three hours on Domain 4. Build two virtual networks with non-overlapping ranges, peer them and watch one link show Initiated until you create the other. Add an NSG to one subnet with a deny rule, test with IP flow verify, read the deciding rule name, then add a lower-numbered allow and test again. Deploy Azure Bastion (the Developer SKU, where your region offers it, is enough for one VM) and connect to a VM without a public IP. Create a private endpoint for the storage account's blob service, link the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone, and compare nslookup results before and after. Add a route table with a route to a nonexistent appliance and check next hop and effective routes. If time remains, put two VMs behind an internal Standard Load Balancer with a probe and break the probe with an NSG deny.

concepts.heading: Sunday Evening: Monitoring and Backup
concepts.body: Spend the last two hours on Domain 5. Create a Log Analytics workspace, a data collection rule for performance counters and event logs, and associate it with a lab VM so the portal installs the Azure Monitor Agent. After data arrives, run a KQL query that summarizes CPU by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) and renders a timechart. Create a metric alert with an action group that emails you, then an alert processing rule that suppresses it for an hour. Create a Recovery Services vault in the VM's region, check the storage redundancy before protecting anything, back up the VM on demand, and use File Recovery to copy one file back. Then stop protection, delete the data and find the item in soft-deleted state. Finish by deleting every lab resource group and checking the budget view.

examPoints: A question that describes a portal error such as a policy deny, a lock refusal or an access denied message is testing settings you can trigger yourself in a lab and remember by sight.
A question about ordering steps, such as peering both sides, protecting a VM after setting redundancy, or running what-if before create, is testing workflow memory that hands-on practice builds best.

quiz.q: During the lab, a learner wants to pause for the night so the lab VM stops incurring compute charges but keeps its disks. What should the learner do?
choices: Shut down the operating system from inside the VM, which deallocates the VM and releases its compute
Delete the VM's network interface, which stops compute billing while keeping the VM and its disks in place
Apply a ReadOnly lock to the resource group, which pauses every running resource until the lock is removed
Select Stop on the VM in the portal, which deallocates it while its managed disks remain in the subscription
quiz.explain: Stopping from the portal deallocates the VM, so compute charges stop while the disks remain. Choice A is tempting because the VM appears off, but shutting down from inside the guest leaves the VM allocated and still billed for compute.

quiz.q: In the lab, an administrator assigns the allowed locations policy to rg-lab and then tries to create a storage account in another region. What should the administrator expect to see?
choices: The account is created and later flagged as noncompliant, because policies only report on existing resources
The deployment is denied with a message that names the policy assignment that blocked the request
The account is moved automatically to the allowed region, because the policy remediates the location setting
The deployment waits for approval from an Owner, because policy denials can be overridden on request
quiz.explain: The allowed locations definition uses the Deny effect, so Resource Manager rejects the request and names the assignment. Choice A is tempting because it describes how audit effects behave, but the allowed locations policy denies the request instead of only flagging it.

days.recap: A two-day lab that triggers real errors in each domain, from policy denials and SAS revocation to peering states, IP flow verify and soft-deleted backups, turns exam scenarios into things you have already seen.

days.title: Final Review: Exam Format, Commonly Confused Pairs, and Test-Day Plan

concepts.heading: Know the Exam Format
concepts.body: AZ-104 gives you 100 minutes for the assessment, and you pass with a scaled score of 700 or greater. Microsoft does not publish the number of questions, so pace yourself by time, checking at the halfway mark that you are about halfway through. The domains are identities and governance 20 to 25 percent, storage 15 to 20 percent, compute 20 to 25 percent, virtual networking 15 to 20 percent, and monitor and maintain 10 to 15 percent. The exam is proctored, and Microsoft says you may have interactive components to complete; its exam experience page also mentions case studies and, on some exams, labs. Try the exam sandbox, linked from the certification page, to see how the item types look. Most questions cover generally available features, so study current names such as Microsoft Entra ID.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Identity, Governance, and Storage
concepts.body: Azure roles such as Contributor act on resources, while Microsoft Entra roles such as User Administrator act on the directory. Owner can assign roles; Contributor cannot. Azure Policy decides what may exist, RBAC decides who may act, and locks block deletion or changes even for Owners, with ReadOnly also breaking some read-like operations such as listing storage keys. Security groups grant access, while Microsoft 365 groups add shared mailboxes and files. An ad hoc SAS cannot be revoked except by rotating the key, while a SAS tied to a stored access policy can be revoked by changing the policy. LRS keeps copies in one datacenter, ZRS across zones, GRS and GZRS add a secondary region. Soft delete restores deleted blobs; versioning restores overwritten ones. Review days 1 to 12 for any pair that still feels shaky.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Compute and Networking
concepts.body: Availability sets spread VMs across fault and update domains in one datacenter; availability zones spread them across datacenters. Scale up changes the App Service plan tier; scale out adds instances. Slot settings stay with the slot during a swap; other settings move with the app. Incremental deployments leave unlisted resources alone; complete mode deletes them from the resource group. Encryption at host is the recommended choice for new VMs; Azure Disk Encryption, which encrypts inside the guest, retires on 15 September 2028 and is not recommended. Service endpoints keep the public endpoint with the subnet's identity; private endpoints give a private IP reachable from on-premises. Next hop shows routing; IP flow verify shows NSG decisions. NSG rules stop at the lowest matching number. Peering is not transitive, and gateway transit needs a setting on each side. Azure Backup puts the vault in the VM's region, Site Recovery outside the source region.

concepts.heading: Use an Error Log
concepts.body: In the last days, more questions help less than understanding the ones you missed. Keep a simple error log with three columns: the question's topic, the rule you did not know, and the clue in the stem you should have noticed. For example: topic Bastion, rule native client needs Standard or Premium, clue "from their own terminal". After every practice set, add new rows and reread the whole log, and redo missed questions after a day without looking at the answer. Group entries by domain to see which day of this plan to revisit; if one domain fills half the log, spend the next session on it and its review day. Use the question bank's domain filter and mock exam with the one section option to drill a weak domain, and stop adding new material the evening before the exam.

concepts.heading: Test-Day Plan
concepts.body: The day before, run a short timed mock, reread your error log and sleep. On the day, check your ID and your testing setup early; for an online proctored exam, clear the desk and test the system ahead of time. During the exam, read the last sentence of each scenario first so you know what is being asked, then look for the deciding clue: a region, a SKU, a word such as on-premises, without downtime or minimum administrative effort. Eliminate answers that use retired features such as Basic SKUs or the Log Analytics agent. If a question takes too long, choose your best answer, mark it for review and move on, and answer every item, because an unanswered item never scores. If you do not pass, review the score report by domain; Microsoft allows a retake after 24 hours for a first failure.

examPoints: A question that lists RBAC, Azure Policy and resource locks together is testing the difference between who may act, what may exist, and what cannot be deleted or changed.
A question with a single deciding clue, such as on-premises access, no downtime or a specific SKU feature, is testing whether you read for that clue before choosing among look-alike services.

quiz.q: A partner was given an ad hoc SAS URL for a container, and the URL leaked. The team wants to revoke only that access as quickly as possible next time without affecting other apps. What should they use when issuing future SAS tokens?
choices: A SAS linked to a stored access policy on the container, so changing or deleting the policy revokes it
An account SAS with a short expiry time, so that rotating either account key immediately revokes it
A ReadOnly lock on the storage account, so that leaked SAS tokens can only read and never write data
A user delegation SAS with no expiry, so that removing the partner's guest account revokes the token
quiz.explain: A SAS tied to a stored access policy can be revoked by editing or deleting the policy, without touching account keys. Choice B is tempting because key rotation does revoke SAS tokens, but it breaks every other app and token signed with that key.

quiz.q: An administrator must run a VM scenario with the least risk: replace a VM's broken disks in place from last night's backup, and in a separate case prove regional recovery without downtime. Which pair of actions is correct?
choices: Create new virtual machine from backup for the first case, and a planned failover with Site Recovery for the second
Restore disks from backup for the first case, and a re-protect operation in Site Recovery for the second
Replace existing from backup for the first case, and a test failover with Site Recovery for the second
File Recovery from backup for the first case, and Cross Region Restore of the latest snapshot for the second
quiz.explain: Replace existing swaps the disks on the existing VM, and test failover proves recovery without affecting production or replication. Choice A is tempting because both are real recovery actions, but Create new builds a different VM and a planned failover moves production rather than testing it.

days.recap: AZ-104 is 100 minutes with a scaled pass mark of 700 and an unpublished question count; drill the confused pairs, read each scenario for its deciding clue, avoid retired features, and answer every item before submitting.
